steps.headline: Choose a primitive for each of four needs.

workedSteps.text: A service must keep a file's contents secret from anyone who steals the disk. Secrecy for parties who share a key calls for symmetric encryption, such as AES in an authenticated mode, which also detects any change to the data.
A site publishes a download and wants users to detect corruption. A fingerprint with no key is enough, so a hash such as SHA-256 is the tool.
A vendor wants users to know that an update really came from the vendor. Only the vendor should be able to produce a valid mark, and users must be able to check it.
A site must store users' passwords so that a stolen database resists offline guessing, which the earlier lesson answered with a slow salted hash.

steps.headline: Choose a primitive for a fifth need.

workedSteps.text: Two services inside one company already share a secret key, and one of them sends instructions to the other.
The receiving service must be able to detect any message that someone without the key made or changed.
The choice lies among the primitives that use a key.

lead.text: Everything above comes with a rule: do not invent your own cryptography, and do not assemble the pieces in ways that nobody has examined. A designer cannot see their own mistakes, and the algorithms in use, such as AES and SHA-256, were chosen after years of open attack by researchers trying to break them. Encrypting each block independently, which is called ECB mode, leaks patterns in the data, and reusing a one-time value, a nonce, under the same key can undo the secrecy of a whole stream.

afterFigure.text: The advice is to use a well-reviewed library through an interface that makes the safe choice the default, with an authenticated mode such as AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305, which protects secrecy and detects change together. Keys must come from a cryptographically secure random generator, and not from a timestamp or a phrase typed by hand, and they are stored apart from the data they protect.

reveal.text: An encoding hides nothing from anyone who knows its name, and passwords need a slow salted hash instead.

lessons.orientation: Tell symmetric encryption, hashing, signatures and key exchange apart, and say why you do not invent your own.
lessons.nextAction: See how TLS uses these primitives to protect a connection, and read a certificate chain.

blocks.text: According to Suetonius, Julius Caesar protected confidential letters by writing D for A and each following letter three places along, so that HELLO would appear as KHOOR. The scheme fails for two reasons that still organise the whole subject. A reader who learns the rule can read every message, and a reader who does not know it need only try the 25 possible shifts to find the one that yields words.

Modern cryptography answers both weaknesses. It assumes that the enemy knows the method and rests everything on a key, and it makes the number of possible keys so large that trying them all is out of reach.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to run a small cipher by hand, say which primitive suits a need, and explain why published, reviewed algorithms are the safe choice.
intro.whyItMatters: Choosing the wrong primitive, such as encoding where encryption is needed, is a common and avoidable fault.

recap.keyIdea: Security rests on a key and on published, reviewed algorithms, and each primitive has its own purpose: secrecy, fingerprinting, signing or agreeing keys.

blocks.text: A cipher is safe only when its key space is too large to search and when it stays secure with the method public, which is Kerckhoffs's principle. Symmetric encryption keeps data secret with a shared key, a hash gives a fixed-size fingerprint, and asymmetric keys serve for key exchange and signatures, so the choice of primitive follows the need. Because details such as the mode and the nonce decide the result, you use a vetted library and never your own design.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson puts these tools together in TLS, which protects most connections on the web, and shows how a certificate chain tells a browser whom it is talking to.

lessons.title: TLS and certificates

lead.text: **Transport Layer Security**, or **TLS**, is the protocol under HTTPS, and it gives a connection three properties from the first lesson. The data is kept secret from anyone watching the network, which is confidentiality, any change to it on the way is detected, which is integrity, and the client learns that it is talking to the server that owns the name it asked for, which is authentication of the server. The current version is TLS 1.3, published as RFC 8446 in August 2018.

afterFigure.text: The padlock in the address bar reports exactly this and nothing more: the connection is encrypted to the site named in the address. It says nothing about whether the site is honest, since a criminal can obtain a certificate for a lookalike name as easily as anyone else, and a padlock on a phishing page is common.

lead.text: The client begins with a **ClientHello** that lists the algorithms it supports, carries its half of a key exchange, and names the site it wants, `shop.example.com`. The server answers with a **ServerHello** that chooses an algorithm and carries its own half. From these two halves both sides compute the same secret, which has never crossed the network, and every message after the second is encrypted.

afterFigure.text: The server then sends its certificate together with a signature, made with the private key that matches the certificate's public key, over the handshake so far. Only the real owner of the name can produce it, and this is what authenticates the server. Each side sends a **Finished** message that confirms the whole handshake arrived unaltered, and application data then flows under a symmetric key after one round trip. The key exchange uses fresh temporary keys for every connection, so a server key stolen later cannot decrypt traffic that was recorded earlier, a property called **forward secrecy**.

reveal.text: The expensive public-key steps happen once per connection, and the cheap symmetric cipher does the bulk of the work.

lead.text: A **certificate** is a signed statement that a particular public key belongs to a particular name, such as `shop.example.com`. It records the name, the public key, the dates between which it is valid and the issuer, and the issuer signs the whole of it with its own private key. The issuer is a **certificate authority**, or CA, an organisation that checks that the applicant controls the name before signing. A browser or operating system ships with a **trust store**, a list of root CAs that it trusts without further proof.

afterFigure.text: Roots rarely sign sites directly, since their keys are kept offline and guarded, so a root signs an intermediate CA and the intermediate signs the site's certificate, called the leaf. The server sends the leaf and the intermediate, and the client checks each signature in turn: the leaf was signed by the intermediate's key, the intermediate was signed by the root's key, and the root is in the trust store. If any link is missing or does not verify, the chain fails and the connection is refused.

diagram.caption: The certificates in a chain. Use the buttons to read each one.

reveal.text: Trust starts at the root that the client chose to hold, and each verified signature carries it one link further.
The next screen lists all four checks, and the error code that each failure produces.

lead.text: When a browser receives a chain, it makes four checks, and a failure in any one stops the connection. The **name** in the certificate must match the site that was requested, the **dates** must include today, the **chain** must lead to a root in the trust store, and the certificate must not have been **revoked**, which means withdrawn by its issuer before its end date, for example after a private key was stolen. Each failure has a recognisable code.

afterFigure.text: Expiry deserves the most attention in practice, because it is the failure that operators cause themselves. The industry's rules have been shortening the longest life a public certificate may have, from 398 days to 200 days in March 2026 and to 47 days by 2029, many are already issued for 90 days or less, and automated renewal through the ACME protocol is now common, so that nobody has to remember. A wrong name, an untrusted issuer or a missing intermediate point to a configuration fault on the server, and a revoked certificate is found by asking the issuer.

diagram.alt: Four views of the four checks a browser makes on a certificate: name, dates, chain and revocation. Each view shows one failing check with the error code the browser reports.
diagram.caption: The four checks and the failure each one produces. Use the buttons to see the errors.

steps.headline: Diagnose three connections that fail, using the error that each browser reports.

workedSteps.text: The first browser reports `NET::ERR_CERT_DATE_INVALID`. The certificate's last valid day was 30 May 2026, and the check is made on 2 June 2026, so the dates check has failed.

The second reports `NET::ERR_CERT_COMMON_NAME_INVALID`. The certificate names `www.example.com`, but the visitor asked for `api.example.com`, so the name check fails, and the fix is a certificate that lists the api name.
The third reports `NET::ERR_CERT_AUTHORITY_INVALID`. The chain ends at a CA that is not in the client's trust store, or the server failed to send its intermediate, so the chain check fails.
In all three cases the browser refuses the connection, since one failed check is enough.

steps.headline: Check how long a certificate valid until 30 May 2026 has left on 20 April 2026.

workedSteps.text: April has 30 days, and the days left in it are the ones after the 20th.
May then adds every day up to the 30th.
The days remaining are the days left in April together with the days of May.

reveal.text: The checks establish whom you are connected to, and judging whether that party can be trusted is still up to the user.

lessons.orientation: Explain how a TLS connection proves the server's name and protects the data, and diagnose the common certificate failures.
lessons.nextAction: Find and rank vulnerabilities, and build the habits that keep new code from adding them.

blocks.text: A browser that cannot trust a site's certificate stops and shows a full-page warning that carries a code such as `NET::ERR_CERT_DATE_INVALID`, and the code is already a diagnosis: the certificate's dates did not hold.

Those checks are made during the TLS handshake, the short exchange that opens every secure connection, and they rest on certificates, each signed by an authority that the browser already trusts or by one that such an authority has vouched for.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say what each step of a TLS handshake does, trace a certificate chain to its root, and name the check behind each common warning.
intro.whyItMatters: Most certificate trouble is an expiry or a wrong name, and the browser's error code says which.

recap.keyIdea: TLS authenticates the server with a certificate chain, agrees keys by key exchange, and protects the data with a symmetric key, so each warning is one failed check.

blocks.text: A TLS handshake agrees on keys, proves the server's name with a certificate and a signature, and then switches to a fast symmetric cipher, which gives confidentiality, integrity and a named server. A certificate is trusted when a chain of signatures leads to a root in the client's trust store, and a connection fails when the name, the dates, the chain or revocation check does not hold, which the browser's error code states.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson takes up the weaknesses that sit in the code and software itself, and how to rank them and fix the worst first.

lessons.title: Vulnerabilities and secure development

lead.text: A **CVE**, short for Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures, is an identifier of the form CVE-year-number that everyone uses for the same publicly known flaw, so that a scanner report, a vendor advisory and a news story can all be matched. The rating is a **CVSS** score, from the Common Vulnerability Scoring System, which turns a flaw's technical properties into a **base score** from 0.0 to 10.0.

afterFigure.text: The score comes from a short vector of metrics: how the flaw is reached, over a network or only locally, how complex the attack is, whether the attacker needs an account, whether a user has to do something, and how badly confidentiality, integrity and availability are affected. Scores are grouped into qualitative bands: None for 0.0, Low for 0.1 to 3.9, Medium for 4.0 to 6.9, High for 7.0 to 8.9 and Critical for 9.0 to 10.0. The score measures how bad the flaw is in the abstract, and says nothing of how much it matters to you.

reveal.text: The band tells you how bad the flaw is in the abstract, and ranking a patch queue needs more than that.

lead.text: A team that fixed flaws strictly in order of score would sometimes fix the wrong ones first. Consider a 9.8 on a test server that is cut off from every network, and a 7.5 on an internet-facing web server for which attacks are already being seen. The 9.8 would be severe if anyone could reach it, but no one can, while the 7.5 is reachable by everyone and is being used, so the 7.5 comes first. Three questions adjust the score: can an attacker reach the asset, is the flaw known to be exploited, and what would be lost if it were?

afterFigure.text: CISA publishes a Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue of flaws that have been used in real attacks, and FIRST publishes EPSS, an estimate of the probability that a flaw will be exploited in the next thirty days. The figure's second view applies one example rule: multiply the score by an exposure weight, 3 for internet-facing, 2 for internal and 1 for isolated, and add 10 if attacks have been seen.

lead.text: A **secure development lifecycle** places checks through the whole path from idea to operation and not only at the end, which is often called *shifting left*, after the diagrams that draw the pipeline from left to right. In design, a threat model like the one in the second lesson finds faults while they cost a conversation to fix. In coding, a reviewer reads each change for security as well as correctness, and a **secret scan** looks for passwords and keys committed by mistake. At build time, **static analysis** reads the source for known dangerous patterns, and a **dependency scan** compares the libraries that the project uses with a database of known flaws.

afterFigure.text: Later stages test the running system by exercising the application with unexpected input in a test environment, and release checks confirm that settings, such as debug modes and default accounts, are safe before anything is deployed. The second view of the figure shows why the early stages pay: a key committed by mistake is stopped at the code stage by the secret scan, whereas without it the key reaches operation and must be treated as stolen and replaced.

reveal.text: The scan reads the list of libraries and versions, which a lock file or a bill of materials provides.

lead.text: Most modern applications are mostly other people's code, so the team that ships the application owns the flaws in every library it includes, and has to know what it includes. A list of components, called a **software bill of materials**, and lock files that pin versions make that possible. Scanners help, but they find known classes of flaw and they report false positives, so each finding needs triage to confirm that the flaw can be reached in this application, and a clean scan means only that nothing known was found.

afterFigure.text: Sometimes the flaw is found by someone outside, and how the team receives the report matters. In **coordinated disclosure** the finder reports privately, the vendor is given time to fix, and the details are published when a patch exists. A team makes this possible by publishing a **security.txt** file, a plain text file at `/.well-known/security.txt` that gives a contact address and the disclosure policy, as described in RFC 9116.

steps.headline: Rank five findings with the example rule: score × exposure weight, plus 10 if attacks have been seen.

workedSteps.text: The weights are 3 for internet-facing, 2 for internal and 1 for isolated. Finding B, a 7.5 on an internet-facing server that is being attacked, scores 7.5 × 3 + 10.
Finding E, an 8.1 on an internal database with no attacks seen, scores 8.1 × 2.
Finding A is the 9.8 on an isolated test server, so its weight is 1 and nothing is added.
Findings D and C, the 4.3 on the printer and the 3.1 on the laptop, are both internal, so each is multiplied by 2.
Sorting from the highest priority gives the patch order.

steps.headline: Score a sixth finding, F: a 6.4 on an internet-facing server, with attacks seen.

workedSteps.text: The server is internet-facing, so the weight is 3.
The rule multiplies the score by the weight.
Attacks have been seen, so the extra 10 is added after the multiplication.

reveal.text: The scanner can test for what it knows, and logic faults, such as a missing ownership check, usually need a person to find them.

lessons.orientation: Read a CVSS severity, rank patches by exposure as well as score, and place security checks in the development process.
lessons.nextAction: Read the logs that record an attack, and judge how quickly a defender notices one.

blocks.text: A flaw in an upload feature may be recorded as CVE-2026-99999, an invented entry, with a score of 9.8 and a one-line description, and at 9.8 it reads as an emergency. Whether it is one depends on two things that the number does not contain: whether anyone can reach the vulnerable feature, and whether anyone is already using it.
Reading a score together with what it leaves out lets you put a list of findings in the order that removes the most risk first, which is often not the order of their scores.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to place a CVSS score in its band, order a list of findings by exposure and evidence, and name the checks that belong at each stage of delivery.
intro.whyItMatters: A patch queue ordered by score alone puts effort in the wrong place surprisingly often.

recap.keyIdea: A CVSS score rates technical severity only, so patches are ranked by adding exposure and evidence of attacks, and checks are placed through the whole pipeline.

blocks.text: A CVE names a public flaw and its CVSS base score places it in a band from Low to Critical, but the score omits who can reach the system and whether attacks have been seen, which is why a lower score on an exposed system can outrank a higher one on an isolated system. Secure development adds checks at every stage, from threat modelling to dependency and secret scans, and a team that owns its dependencies and publishes a `security.txt` file can act on reports quickly.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns to detection: how the logs that a system keeps show an attack, and how long a defender takes to notice one.

lessons.title: Logging and detection

lead.text: A useful security log entry answers five questions: when it happened, who acted, what they did, where the request came from, and whether it succeeded. The events worth recording are authentication, both successful and failed, access to sensitive data, changes to accounts, permissions and configuration, and errors that suggest someone is probing the system. NIST's guide to log management, SP 800-92, stresses that a log is useful only when its entries are complete, consistent and time-stamped from a clock that can be trusted.

afterFigure.text: A password typed into a failed login, a session token, a card number, or more personal data than the event needs, should never appear in a log. The log also needs protection, since an attacker who controls a server often edits or deletes its local log to hide the visit. Entries should therefore be sent, as they are written, to a separate log server that the first machine cannot change, with access limited and a retention period fixed in advance.

reveal.text: Support staff can still find the account from its identifier, and the entry can leave out the details that the event does not need.

lead.text: Most lines are ordinary: bob and carol sign in once from their usual addresses. Between 10:01:00 and 10:02:50, however, the same address, 203.0.113.9, fails against the account alice eleven times, about ten seconds apart, and at 10:03:01 the same address succeeds. People do not mistype a password eleven times at that steady rhythm, so the pattern points to automated guessing, and the success at the end suggests that it worked.

afterFigure.text: Reading a log in this way means asking the same few questions of every cluster of lines: is it one account or many, one source or many, a human rhythm or a machine one, and what happened next. A success after a burst of failures is the moment the incident begins, so the defender looks at what alice's account did from 10:03:01 onwards, such as a changed password, a new mail-forwarding rule or a login to another system, and treats the account as compromised until shown otherwise.

reveal.text: The count and the spacing of failures together say whether a person or a program was typing.
No traveller can do that, which is the idea behind the rule that the next screen names.

lead.text: A **detection rule** is a condition over the logs that raises an alert. The simplest is a **threshold**: five failed logins for one account within two minutes. A rule for **impossible travel** compares a user's consecutive logins and alerts when the distance between them, divided by the time, would need a speed that no traveller could reach, which is the arithmetic behind the last question. A rule for a **new administrator** alerts when a privileged account is created, or an ordinary account is given privileges, outside an approved change, since attackers who have gained access often create their own. Rules like these compare events with a **baseline** of normal behaviour, and **correlation** combines sources, for instance a login alert followed within minutes by a large download, which is a stronger signal than either alone.

afterFigure.text: Each rule is a guess about what is abnormal, and guesses are sometimes wrong. A rule that fires on a traveller who really did fly, or on an administrator hired this morning, raises a **false positive**, while one that stays silent during a real attack is a false negative. Tuning narrows a rule until most of its alerts deserve attention, for example by ignoring a known scanner's address or by raising a threshold slightly. Leaving a noisy rule untouched leads to **alert fatigue**: when analysts see hundreds of alerts that come to nothing, they start to close them without reading, and the one real alert is closed with the rest.

diagram.alt: Three detection rules. A threshold rule fires on eleven failed logins in under two minutes. An impossible-travel rule fires on logins from London and New York thirty minutes apart. A new-administrator rule fires when an account is made an admin outside a change window.

reveal.text: The fifth failure in the window is the one that raises the alert, so the defender hears about it about two minutes after it begins.

lead.text: **Dwell time** is the time from an intruder's first malicious action to the moment that the defender detects it. The figure's timeline follows an intrusion that starts at 09:05, when a staff member opens a phishing link, and is detected at 14:20, which gives a dwell time of 5 hours 15 minutes, or 315 minutes.

afterFigure.text: Dwell time matters because the stages from the third lesson take time. The second view moves the detection to 09:50, 45 minutes after the start, and the stages after that point never happen. A shorter dwell time therefore means a smaller loss.

diagram.alt: A timeline from 09:00 to 15:00 with an intrusion that begins at 09:05. Events are a link opened at 09:05, persistence at 09:40, a move to the file server at 11:30 and data copied at 13:10. In the first view it is detected at 14:20, a dwell time of 315 minutes. In the second it is detected at 09:50, a dwell time of 45 minutes, and the later events do not happen.

steps.headline: Work out the dwell time for an intrusion that starts at 10:25 and is detected at 16:50 on the same day.

workedSteps.text: Convert each time to minutes after midnight, so that the subtraction takes a single step. 10:25 is 10 × 60 + 25 minutes.
Convert the detection time in the same way. 16:50 is 16 hours and 50 minutes.
Subtract the start from the detection time.
Convert back for the report: 385 minutes is 6 whole hours and 25 minutes over.

steps.headline: Work out the dwell time when the intrusion starts at 22:40 and is detected at 03:10 the next morning.

workedSteps.text: The part before midnight runs from 22:40 to 24:00, which is 1440 − 1360 minutes.
The part after midnight runs from 00:00 to 03:10, which is 3 × 60 + 10 minutes.
The dwell time is the part before midnight together with the part after it.

reveal.text: The record of the visit has to live where the visitor cannot reach it.

lessons.orientation: Decide what to log, read a short log for an attack, name the main kinds of detection rule, and measure dwell time.
lessons.nextAction: Run the first hour of an incident, from deciding what happened to deciding what to contain.

blocks.text: At 10:03 a user called alice signs in successfully from an address she has never used. A single successful login looks like every other, but the lines before it do not: in the two minutes before, that same address failed eleven times against her account, about ten seconds apart. A log is a record of events, and it becomes a defence when someone, or something, reads it for patterns like this one soon enough to act.

That reading can be done by a rule that watches the logs and raises an alert, so that an intrusion can be noticed while it is still under way, and the time between an intruder's first action and the alert can be measured in minutes.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say what an entry should and should not contain, spot a guessing attack in a short log, and compute dwell time in minutes.
intro.whyItMatters: Most intrusions leave a trail in the logs, and detection depends on someone reading it in time.

recap.keyIdea: Log who did what, when, from where and with what result, keep secrets out and copies elsewhere, and judge a defence by how quickly it detects an intruder.

blocks.text: A log entry records when, who, what, from where and the result, leaves out secrets and is sent to a server that the first machine cannot change. Rules such as a threshold, impossible travel and a new administrator turn the lines into alerts, and tuning keeps them few enough to be read. The time between an intruder's first action and its detection is the dwell time, and shortening it stops the later stages of an intrusion from happening.

recap.nextHook: The last lesson uses all of this in the first hour of an incident: what to decide, in what order, and what to contain first.

lessons.title: Incident response

lead.text: NIST's guide to incident handling, SP 800-61, which dates from August 2012 in its second revision, divides the work into four phases. **Preparation** comes first and covers the roles, contact lists, runbooks, logging and tested backups that exist before any incident. **Detection and analysis** confirms that something is wrong, decides how far it extends and how serious it is, and starts the record. **Containment, eradication and recovery** stops the spread, removes the cause and restores normal service. **Post-incident activity** reviews what happened and feeds the answers back into preparation.

afterFigure.text: A common mistake is to think that response starts when an incident does. What decides how the first hour goes is mostly settled beforehand: whether the on-call engineer knows whom to call, whether the runbook says what isolating a server means in this network, and whether the last backup was ever restored in a test. Revision 3 of the guide, issued in 2025, aligns incident response with the functions of the Cybersecurity Framework met in the first lesson, so that it is treated as part of managing cybersecurity risk as a whole.

diagram.alt: Four phases of incident handling in a loop: preparation, detection and analysis, containment, eradication and recovery, and post-incident activity, with an arrow from the last back to the first. Each view highlights one phase and lists example actions.
diagram.caption: The four phases in a loop. Use the buttons to see example actions for each one.

reveal.text: The review turns what happened into changes with owners and dates, and those changes go back into preparation.

lead.text: Once an incident is confirmed, the priority is to stop it growing. **Isolating a host** cuts it off from the network, which stops it spreading to other machines or sending data out. **Disabling an account** stops anyone using a stolen credential, wherever they are. **Blocking an address** stops traffic to or from a known attacker address, though an attacker can usually change address.

afterFigure.text: Containment has a second duty, which is to keep the evidence. Switching a suspect machine off loses the contents of its memory, which may hold the malicious program and the keys it uses, and wiping it destroys what would show how the attacker got in and what else they touched. Containment is followed by **eradication**, which removes the cause, for example by resetting stolen credentials and deleting malicious programs from every host, and then by **recovery**, which restores service from clean backups and watches closely for a return. A restore loses whatever changed since the last backup, so the backup schedule sets how much work can be lost, and every action is written down with its time, so that the team ends with a timeline.

diagram.alt: Three ways to contain an incident: isolating a host, disabling an account and blocking an address. For each, the view shows what it stops, what it leaves open, and what happens to evidence.
diagram.caption: Three containment options. Use the buttons to compare what each stops and what it leaves open.

reveal.text: The attacker changes address and machine freely, so the thing to cut off is the account that the stolen password opens.

lead.text: In the first hour of a serious incident, a small team needs defined roles. An **incident commander** makes the decisions and keeps the others from working at cross purposes, a technical lead directs the investigation and the containment, a scribe records every action and finding with its time, and a communications lead handles managers, staff and, where the law requires, regulators and customers. Some laws set deadlines, such as the 72 hours that the European data protection regulation allows, from the moment an organisation becomes aware of a breach of personal data, to notify the supervisory authority, so the time at which the team became aware is itself something to record.

afterFigure.text: The figure compares two first hours that begin with the same alert. In the second, someone wipes the server at once. The wipe removes the evidence of the entry route, the attacker is still inside, and a second host starts encrypting at 02:30. The same effort produces a worse outcome, because the order was wrong: the cleaning came before the containment.

diagram.alt: Two versions of the first hour after the same ransomware alert at 02:00. In the first the team confirms, isolates the server and disables the account, scopes three hosts and has a restore plan by 03:00. In the second someone wipes the server, a second host starts encrypting, and by 03:00 there is no containment and no known entry route.
diagram.caption: The same alert, handled in two ways. Use the buttons to compare the two hours.

reveal.text: A shorter interval between backups loses less work, at the price of storing and testing more of them.

lead.text: A **post-incident review** is a meeting, held within days while memories are fresh, that builds the timeline from the records and asks what happened, why it was possible, what worked and what must change. It is **blameless**: it does not ask who made a mistake, because a person who made a mistake did so inside a system that allowed it, and a team that fears blame hides facts that the next review needs.

The output is a short written account and a list of changes, each with an owner and a date: a missing alert gets a new detection rule, a stale contact list gets a monthly check, a backup that took too long to restore gets a faster design. The changes then go back into preparation, which closes the loop of four phases drawn at the start of the lesson.

steps.headline: Take a ransomware alert through the phases in order, from 02:00 on a shared file server.

workedSteps.text: At 02:00 an alert reports files being renamed with an unfamiliar extension on the server. The first task is detection and analysis: confirm that the alert is real, say which host and which account are involved, and open an incident record with the time.

Once ransomware is confirmed at 02:10, the spread has to be stopped before anything is cleaned. Isolate the server from the network, leaving it powered on to keep its memory, and disable the account that was used.
Preserve the evidence before anything is changed: copy the logs to the separate log server, capture the memory, and note each action with its time.
Eradication removes the cause. The stolen credential is reset, the malicious program is deleted from every infected host, and the route in is closed.
Recovery restores the service from a clean backup, with monitoring turned up, and returns hosts to the network one at a time.
Afterwards the blameless review records what happened and changes the controls, which feeds the next round of preparation.

reveal.text: Speed matters, and the fastest safe action is isolation, which stops the spread and keeps the evidence.

lessons.orientation: Lead the first hour of an incident through the NIST phases, contain it without losing evidence, and hold a blameless review.
lessons.nextAction: You can now describe how a system is attacked, judge its defences from risk to detection, and run the first hour when one of them fails.

blocks.text: At 02:00 a monitoring system raises an alert: files on a shared server are being renamed with an unfamiliar extension, one every few seconds. The on-call engineer has three questions to answer before anything else, and each is far easier if it was answered earlier: who must be woken, whether the server should be switched off, and where the last good backup is.

NIST's guide to incident handling, SP 800-61, divides the work into four phases that start long before the alert and end with a review afterwards, and taking them in order is what keeps a team from cleaning a machine before it has stopped the spread.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to put the phases in order, choose between isolating, disabling and blocking, and write a review that produces changes with owners and dates.
intro.whyItMatters: The first hour's decisions are mostly made in advance, and a clear order of actions protects the evidence.

recap.keyIdea: Prepare before an incident, contain it without destroying evidence, and review it without blame, so that each incident improves the next response.

blocks.text: The lifecycle runs from preparation through detection and analysis and through containment, eradication and recovery to post-incident activity, and the last phase feeds the first. Containment stops the spread by isolating a host, disabling an account or blocking an address, and it keeps the evidence, so a suspect machine is isolated and left powered on and not wiped. A blameless review then turns the timeline into changes with owners and dates.

questions.prompt: A stolen laptop holds an unencrypted customer list, and the thief reads it. The company keeps other copies of the list. Which property of the list has been lost?
hints: Ask what the thief was able to do with the list: read it, change it, or stop others using it.
The company can still open its other copies. Which of the three things did the thief not do?
questions.onCorrect: The thief only read the list, so nothing was changed and the owner can still use it. Only confidentiality is lost.

choices.label: Integrity, because the list is no longer where its owner keeps it
Confidentiality, because someone with no right to it could read it
Availability, because the company has lost the laptop that held the list

acceptedIdeas: Confidentiality, because someone with no right to it could read it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Confidentiality, because someone with no right to it could read it

misconceptions.feedback: Integrity is lost when information is changed in a way its owners did not intend. The thief only read the list.
The company keeps other copies, so the list can still be used when it is needed. The harm is that a stranger has read it.

questions.prompt: A flood of orders crashes a shop's website. Each crash costs the shop $10,000 in lost sales, and crashes happen 3 times a year on average. Roughly what does this cost the shop in an average year?
hints: Each crash costs the same amount.
Think about what three crashes cost together.
questions.onCorrect: One crash costs 10,000 and there are 3 a year, so the yearly cost is 10,000 × 3 = 30,000 dollars, a quantity the next screen names.

choices.label: About $10,000, the cost of a single crash
About $3,300, the cost of a crash shared over the three
About $30,000, three times the cost of a crash

acceptedIdeas: About $30,000, three times the cost of a crash
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About $30,000, three times the cost of a crash

misconceptions.feedback: That is what one crash costs, and the shop has three of them in an average year, each costing as much as the first.
Dividing spreads one crash's cost across three, but each of the three crashes costs $10,000 on its own, so the costs add up.

questions.prompt: The control in the example saves $18,000 a year and costs $9,000. Why is it worth buying?
hints: Compare the two yearly figures, the saving and the cost.
Ask what is left after the cost has been paid out of the saving.
questions.onCorrect: The net gain is 18,000 - 9,000 = 9,000 a year, and a positive net gain is the usual test for buying a control.

choices.label: Its yearly saving is larger than its yearly cost
It removes the risk of a breach for good
Security spending is justified whatever it costs

acceptedIdeas: Its yearly saving is larger than its yearly cost
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Its yearly saving is larger than its yearly cost

misconceptions.feedback: The rate falls from 0.2 to 0.05, so a risk of 6,000 a year remains. A control reduces risk without removing it.
Spending has to be justified by what it saves or by another stated duty. A control that costs more than it saves needs a separate reason.

questions.prompt: With the $2,000 control, the ALE falls from 24,000 to 18,000. What is the net gain in dollars after paying for the control?
hints: Find the saving first, the fall in the ALE.
Subtract the cost of the control from that saving.
The saving is 6,000.
questions.onCorrect: A cheaper control that cuts the rate less can still give a positive gain, here 4,000 a year.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the saving before the cost of the control is taken off.
That is the cost of the control, not what is left after paying it.
That is the ALE that remains with the control in place.

questions.prompt: A control saves $15,000 a year in expected losses and costs $20,000 a year. A data-protection law requires the shop to have it. What is the right decision?
hints: First work out the net gain from the saving and the cost.
Ask whether anything other than the savings could justify spending the money.
questions.onCorrect: The sums say no and the law says yes, so the control is bought and the reason is written down.

choices.label: Skip it, because the cost is larger than the saving it brings
Buy it, and record that the legal duty is the reason for the cost
Buy it, because a control is worth its price whenever a breach is costly

acceptedIdeas: Buy it, and record that the legal duty is the reason for the cost
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Buy it, and record that the legal duty is the reason for the cost

misconceptions.feedback: The numbers argue against it, but a legal duty is a separate reason and ignoring it brings fines on top of the loss.
A control is worth buying when it saves more than it costs or when another duty requires it. A costly breach alone does not show that the control pays for itself.

questions.prompt: A hospital looks back over six incidents from the past year. Which property of the information did each one break?
hints: For each incident, ask whether information was read by the wrong person, changed, or made impossible to use.
A fault or an accident counts too, so do not look only for an attacker.

items.label: A nurse emails a list of patients to the wrong address
items.explanation: A stranger can now read the list. Nothing in it changed and the hospital can still use it.

items.label: A script bug overwrites dosage figures in the pharmacy table
items.explanation: The data was changed in a way its owners did not intend, and no attacker was needed.

items.label: Ransomware locks the records server for two days
items.explanation: The records exist but cannot be used when staff need them.

items.label: A visitor reads patient files over a doctor's shoulder
items.explanation: Someone who is not authorised can see the information.

items.label: An attacker edits a lab result while it travels between two systems
items.explanation: The result arrives altered, so it can no longer be trusted.

items.label: A failed disk takes the booking system offline
items.explanation: No one attacked anything, and the system still cannot be used when it is needed.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The email to the wrong address and the shoulder-surfing visitor are confidentiality, the overwritten dosages and the edited lab result are integrity, and the locked server and the failed disk are availability.

questions.onCorrect: The three properties describe what happens to the information, whether the cause is an attacker, a fault or a mistake.

questions.prompt: A risk report gives the annualised loss expectancy of ransomware as $40,000. A manager reads this as a forecast that ransomware will cost exactly $40,000 this year. What is wrong with that reading?
hints: The ALE is the cost of one loss times how often it happens in a year.
If a $200,000 loss is expected once in five years, what do the other four years cost?
questions.onCorrect: An ALE of $40,000 could be one $200,000 loss in five years with four quiet years between, so it works as a budgeting figure and not a prediction.

choices.label: The figure is the yearly cost of the controls needed to prevent the loss
The figure is the largest loss that ransomware could cause in a single year
The figure averages many years, so one year may cost far more or nothing

acceptedIdeas: The figure averages many years, so one year may cost far more or nothing
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The figure averages many years, so one year may cost far more or nothing

misconceptions.feedback: The cost of controls is a separate number that is compared with the ALE. The ALE itself is the expected yearly loss.
The ALE is an expected value, not a worst case. A bad year can cost much more than the figure, and that is what insurance and backups are for.

questions.prompt: A $6,000 control cuts the rate of a $30,000 loss from 0.4 a year to 0.1. What is the net annual benefit in dollars?
hints: Work out the ALE with and without the control.
Take the control's cost off the saving.
The saving is the fall in the ALE.
questions.onCorrect: A positive net benefit means the control saves more each year than it costs.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The ALE falls from 30,000 × 0.4 = 12,000 to 30,000 × 0.1 = 3,000, a saving of 9,000. Subtracting the 6,000 cost leaves 3,000.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the saving. The control's cost of 6,000 still has to come off.
That is the ALE before the control. The benefit is the fall in the ALE less the cost.

questions.prompt: A clinic's booking system has a web server and a database inside the clinic's own network, which is the trust boundary. Which of these flows crosses the boundary?
hints: For each flow, decide whether its two ends are on the same side of the boundary.
A laptop used by staff but connecting from home is outside the clinic's network.
questions.onCorrect: Data from outside may have been written by someone less trusted, so crossing flows are examined first.

choices.label: From the web server to the database, over the clinic's switch
From a receptionist's office PC to the web server, on the clinic's network
From a nurse's laptop at home to the web server, over the internet
From the database to its backup disk in the same room

acceptedIdeas: From a nurse's laptop at home to the web server, over the internet
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: From a nurse's laptop at home to the web server, over the internet

misconceptions.feedback: Both ends are inside the clinic's network, so no change of trust lies between them.
The office PC is inside the clinic's network, so this flow stays inside the boundary.
The disk is in the same room and on the same side of the boundary as the database.

questions.prompt: A customer's password appears on a leaked list, and an attacker uses it to sign in to the shop as that customer. Which STRIDE threat is this, and which property does it attack?
hints: The attacker is pretending to be somebody else.
The attacker gains no rights beyond those of the customer whose password they used.
questions.onCorrect: Using a stolen credential makes the attacker appear to be the customer, which is why authentication is the property at stake.

choices.label: Spoofing, which attacks authentication
Elevation of privilege, which attacks authorisation
Tampering, which attacks integrity
Repudiation, which attacks non-repudiation

acceptedIdeas: Spoofing, which attacks authentication
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Spoofing, which attacks authentication

misconceptions.feedback: The attacker has only the customer's own rights. Elevation of privilege would be gaining rights beyond those of the account they are using.
Nothing has been altered. The attacker is pretending to be someone else.
Repudiation is someone denying an action when nothing can prove otherwise. Here the attacker is hiding behind a real customer's identity.

questions.prompt: A flood of requests could shut real customers out of the shop. Which property of the system does that violate?
hints: Think back to the properties in the first lesson, and ask which one is about being able to use the system.
A flood changes nothing and reads nothing. Ask what it does to the customers.
questions.onCorrect: Denial of service is the threat that violates availability, and rate limits are a common response.

acceptedIdeas: Availability
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Availability

choices.label: Confidentiality
Integrity
Non-repudiation
Availability

misconceptions.feedback: Confidentiality concerns who can read information, and nobody has read anything here.
Integrity concerns whether information is changed. A flood changes nothing; it keeps customers from using the shop.
Non-repudiation concerns a person denying something they did, and no one's denial is involved in a flood.

questions.prompt: A threat would need physical access to the shop's office and could expose only a public product list, and fixing it would cost more than the list is worth. What is the sensible response?
hints: Compare the cost of a fix with the harm the threat could do.
Ask what a response costs against what the shop would lose if the threat succeeded.
questions.onCorrect: Accepting is a legitimate decision when the harm is small, as long as the reason and the person who agreed to it are recorded.

choices.label: Remove it by taking the product list down
Transfer it by insuring against it
Accept it, and record why
Reduce it with locks and cameras on the office

acceptedIdeas: Accept it, and record why
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Accept it, and record why

misconceptions.feedback: Locks and cameras cost money to protect a list that is already public, so the control would cost more than the harm it prevents.
Taking the list down would remove the threat, but the shop needs its product list to sell anything, so it would lose far more than the threat could cost.
Insurance costs a premium every year, and there is no loss here worth insuring, since the list is already public.

questions.prompt: A message board keeps no record of who posted what, and a user denies posting an abusive message. Which response addresses that threat?
hints: The user is denying an action, and the system cannot show otherwise.
What would the board need to have kept for it to answer the user?
questions.onCorrect: A record of actions that its users cannot alter lets the board answer a denial, and the lesson on logging returns to it.

choices.label: A limit on how many messages one address may post in a single hour
A log of every post tied to an account, which users cannot edit
Encrypting the connection between the browser and the board
A stronger password rule for new accounts

acceptedIdeas: A log of every post tied to an account, which users cannot edit
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A log of every post tied to an account, which users cannot edit

misconceptions.feedback: A rate limit answers a flood, which is denial of service. It does not show who posted a given message.
Encryption keeps outsiders from reading or changing traffic. It does not give the board a record that the user cannot dispute.
Stronger passwords make spoofing harder, but the user here is not claiming that anyone else posted the message.

questions.prompt: A team lists six threats to its web shop. Which of these three STRIDE threats is each one?
hints: Ask whether the attacker is pretending to be someone, changing data, or gaining rights that the account was never given.
A customer who is correctly identified but does something beyond their role is not spoofing.

items.label: Someone signs in as a customer with a password taken from a leaked list
items.explanation: The attacker pretends to be a customer, so authentication is what fails.

items.label: A fake payment service answers the shop's server and receives the card details
items.explanation: The server has been tricked about who it is talking to.

items.label: A device on the network path changes the price in an order before it arrives
items.explanation: The data is changed without permission on its way, which is a loss of integrity.

items.label: A staff member edits a saved order's total directly in the database
items.explanation: Saved data is changed without anything to show that it should be.

items.label: An ordinary customer opens the admin page by typing its address
items.explanation: The customer gains rights that were never granted, so authorisation is what fails.

items.label: A signed-in customer adds a hidden field to a form and is given staff rights
items.explanation: The account gains privileges beyond its role.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Signing in with a leaked password and the fake payment service are spoofing, the changed price and the edited order total are tampering, and the admin page and the hidden field are elevation of privilege.

questions.onCorrect: Spoofing is about who someone is, tampering is about what happens to data, and elevation of privilege is about what an account may do.

questions.prompt: Where should trust boundaries be drawn on a data-flow diagram?
hints: Ask what a boundary is meant to show about the two sides of it.
Picture two processes that run with the same privileges. Does anything change when data passes between them?
questions.onCorrect: A boundary marks a change in trust or privilege, and data that crosses it deserves a check.

choices.label: Wherever data passes between parts trusted to different degrees
Around every process, to keep each one separate
Only at the firewall, where the network meets the open internet
Only around the database, since that is where data rests

acceptedIdeas: Wherever data passes between parts trusted to different degrees
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Wherever data passes between parts trusted to different degrees

misconceptions.feedback: Boundaries mark changes of trust. Two processes that are trusted equally and run with the same privileges need none between them.
A firewall is one place where trust changes, but a boundary is also needed between a server and a third-party service, or between an ordinary user's privileges and an administrator's.
The database is often inside a boundary, but boundaries are drawn wherever trust changes, wherever that is.

questions.prompt: Two weeks before launch, the team adds an analytics service run by another company, and the browser now sends it each customer's email address. The threat model was signed off last month. What should the team do?
hints: The fourth question of threat modelling asks whether the work is still good enough after a change.
What has been added that the diagram does not yet show?
questions.onCorrect: Each new feature, service or boundary means the diagram is updated and the questions are asked again about what changed.

choices.label: Leave the model as it is, because it was signed off and approved
Ask only about information disclosure, since an email address is the only data involved
Ask the STRIDE questions again only about the flows that were already there
Add the new flow to the diagram and ask the six STRIDE questions about it

acceptedIdeas: Add the new flow to the diagram and ask the six STRIDE questions about it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Add the new flow to the diagram and ask the six STRIDE questions about it

misconceptions.feedback: A new third-party service is a new flow across the boundary, and a model that does not show it is out of date.
The old flows have already been examined. The new flow is the one with no answers yet.
Disclosure matters here, but the flow can also be spoofed, tampered with or flooded, and the point of STRIDE is to ask every question.

questions.prompt: A defender finds a scheduled task that nobody on the team created, set to start a program every night, so that the attacker can return after the machine restarts. Which of the seven stages is this?
hints: The task exists so that access survives a restart.
Of the seven stages, which one is about coming back later and not about getting in?
questions.onCorrect: Persistence mechanisms such as scheduled tasks are a common place to look when cleaning up after an intrusion.

acceptedIdeas: persistence
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: persistence

questions.prompt: One control stops 80% of the attacks that reach it, and a second control stops 80% of those that get past the first. Roughly what share of attacks gets past both?
hints: A control that stops 80% lets 20% through.
The second control sees only what the first let through.
questions.onCorrect: Each control lets 20% through, so 0.2 × 0.2 = 0.04, or 4% of attacks, get past both.

choices.label: Much less than 20%, only a few in every hundred
None, since two controls of 80% cover every attack
About 20%, the same as with one control

acceptedIdeas: Much less than 20%, only a few in every hundred
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Much less than 20%, only a few in every hundred

misconceptions.feedback: The second control acts on the 20% that passed the first and stops most of those too, so fewer get through than with one control.
The second control sees only the attacks that passed the first, so its 80% is a share of a smaller number, and the two percentages cannot be added.

questions.prompt: Why can the pass fractions of the three layers be combined by multiplying them?
hints: Think about what the host layer receives.
If the network layer stops most attacks, how many are left for the next layer to look at?
questions.onCorrect: This holds only when the layers fail for different reasons. Two layers that depend on one password fail together.

choices.label: Each layer sees only what the layer before it let through
Every layer stops the same share of the attacks reaching it
The strongest layer decides the result and the others add nothing

acceptedIdeas: Each layer sees only what the layer before it let through
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each layer sees only what the layer before it let through

misconceptions.feedback: The layers stop different shares, 90%, 70% and 80%. Multiplication works because each acts on what remains.
Every layer contributes. The combined fraction is smaller than that of the strongest layer alone.

questions.prompt: Adding a layer that stops 50% of what reaches it lets 0.5 through. The earlier three layers let through 0.006 of attacks. What percentage gets past all four?
hints: Multiply the earlier fraction by the new layer's pass fraction.
0.006 × 0.5 gives a fraction.
Multiply the fraction by 100 to get a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: Each added layer multiplies the pass fraction by a number below one, though the gain shrinks as the fraction gets small.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the fraction. The question asks for a percentage, so multiply by 100.
That is the percentage for three layers. The fourth layer halves it.

questions.prompt: The database server misses a patch, so the host layer stops nothing. Only the network layer, which stops 90% of what reaches it, and the application layer, which stops 80%, remain. What percentage of attacks gets past both?
hints: Write the pass fraction of each remaining layer.
The host layer no longer changes the result.
Multiply the two pass fractions and give the answer as a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: Losing the host layer raises the passage from 0.6% to 2%, more than three times as much, though the other layers still hold.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The network layer lets 0.1 through and the application layer lets 0.2 through, so 0.1 × 0.2 = 0.02, which is 2%.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the figure with the host layer in place. Without it, one fewer factor is multiplied in.
That multiplies the stopped fractions. Use the fractions that pass.

questions.prompt: A team reports that its network, host and application layers stop 90%, 70% and 80% of attacks, so only 0.6% get through. All three layers accept the same shared administrator password. Why is 0.6% too optimistic?
hints: Multiplying the pass rates assumes that the layers fail for different reasons.
What single thing would an attacker need in order to pass each layer here?
questions.onCorrect: Layers multiply only when they fail independently. Three layers that rest on one password behave like a single layer.

choices.label: One stolen password defeats every layer at once, so they fail together
The pass rate should be the average of the three layers, which comes to 20%
The shared password only matters to the last layer, so 0.6% still holds

acceptedIdeas: One stolen password defeats every layer at once, so they fail together
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: One stolen password defeats every layer at once, so they fail together

misconceptions.feedback: Averaging would ignore that each layer acts on what the one before let through. The product is correct when the layers fail independently, and this is the case where they do not.
A password that every layer accepts lets an attacker through each of them, the last one included.

questions.prompt: A company is broken into through a phishing email. In what order do these six things happen?
hints: The attacker has to learn about the target before the first foothold, and the harm comes last.
A program cannot run on the laptop until the attacker has some access to it, and the program is what makes higher rights possible.

items: The attacker collects staff names and the format of email addresses
An employee types a password into a fake sign-in page
The attacker's program runs on the employee's laptop
A scheduled task is added that starts the program every night
The attacker takes an administrator's token from the laptop
The files on the file server are encrypted

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Reconnaissance comes first, then initial access through the password, then execution of the program, persistence through the scheduled task, privilege escalation with the administrator's token, and impact when the files are encrypted.

questions.onCorrect: Each stage builds on the one before, which is why catching an early stage prevents the later ones.

questions.prompt: You want to scan your employer's website for weaknesses. What do you need from its owner before you start?
hints: Think about what makes access to someone else's system lawful, and what you could show afterwards.
A good intention does not decide whether an act is allowed. Who does?
questions.onCorrect: The permission names the systems, the dates and the methods in scope, so that the test stays inside what the owner allowed.

acceptedIdeas: Written permission that names what you may test
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Written permission that names what you may test

choices.label: Nothing, as long as you only look and change nothing
Written permission that names what you may test
A spoken agreement from a colleague who works on the site
A promise to report anything you find to the owner afterwards

misconceptions.feedback: Unauthorised access is an offence however good the intention, and looking without changing anything is still access.
A spoken agreement leaves nothing to show what was allowed, and a colleague may not be the person entitled to allow it.
A report afterwards cannot undo a scan that the owner never agreed to.

questions.prompt: A scan of the shop's public web server shows `22/tcp open ssh`, `80/tcp open http`, `443/tcp open https` and `5432/tcp open postgresql`. Which line should be fixed first?
hints: Ask which of these services the whole internet has a reason to reach.
Port numbers worth knowing by sight include 5432, which belongs to PostgreSQL.
questions.onCorrect: A database reachable from the internet invites password guessing and attacks on the database software, so it sits behind the web server.

choices.label: `80/tcp open http`, since it carries web traffic without any encryption at all
`22/tcp open ssh`, since it gives remote command access
`5432/tcp open postgresql`, since only the web server needs the database
`443/tcp open https`, since any open port is a weakness

acceptedIdeas: `5432/tcp open postgresql`, since only the web server needs the database
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: `5432/tcp open postgresql`, since only the web server needs the database

misconceptions.feedback: A public website has to answer on port 80, often only to send visitors on to https. It is not the most urgent line.
Port 22 should be limited to the administrators' addresses, but a database open to the internet is the greater exposure.
The shop has to answer on port 443 for its visitors. An open port is a weakness only when nobody needs it open.

questions.prompt: A firewall's rules, in order, are: 1 deny tcp 5432 from any host to db; 2 allow tcp 5432 from web to db; 3 deny all. What happens to a packet from web to db on tcp 5432?
hints: Read the rules from the top.
Ask whether rule 1 matches a packet that comes from the web server.
Once a rule matches, are the later rules read?
questions.onCorrect: A broad rule above a narrow one hides it, so the fix is to put the allow rule for the web server first.

choices.label: Rule 3 denies it, because it ends the list
Rule 2 allows it, because it names the web server exactly
It is allowed, because an allow rule outranks a deny rule
Rule 1 denies it, because it matches first

acceptedIdeas: Rule 1 denies it, because it matches first
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Rule 1 denies it, because it matches first

misconceptions.feedback: Rule 2 would allow it, but the firewall stops at the first rule that matches, and rule 1, which covers any source, matches first.
The packet never reaches rule 3, because rule 1 already matches it and decides.
A firewall gives no rule priority by kind. It reads from the top, and the first rule that matches decides.

questions.prompt: Which rule decides the packet from a host on the internet to the web server on tcp 22?
hints: Go down the list in order and ask whether each rule matches.
Rule 3 allows port 22 only for the office network.
questions.onCorrect: An outside host reaches rule 4 because rule 3 names the office as the only source for ssh.

choices.label: Rule 3, because it names tcp 22 and the web server
Rule 1, because the packet is headed to the web server
Rule 4, because no allow rule above it matches

acceptedIdeas: Rule 4, because no allow rule above it matches
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Rule 4, because no allow rule above it matches

misconceptions.feedback: Rule 3 does name port 22 and the web server, but only for sources in the office network, and this packet comes from outside.
Rule 1 is about tcp 443, and this packet is for tcp 22.

questions.prompt: A café's Wi-Fi uses WEP, hides its network name and allows only listed device addresses. The owner can make one change. Which gives the largest gain in security?
hints: WEP can be broken, and hiding names and filtering addresses do not stop that.
Which of the three measures changes how the traffic itself is protected?
questions.onCorrect: WPA2 or WPA3 with a long passphrase protects the traffic itself, which the other two measures never did.

choices.label: Switch to WPA2 or WPA3 with a long passphrase
Rename the hidden network to something nobody would guess
Cut the list of allowed device addresses down to the staff only

acceptedIdeas: Switch to WPA2 or WPA3 with a long passphrase
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Switch to WPA2 or WPA3 with a long passphrase

misconceptions.feedback: The name is sent in the frames that devices exchange, so hiding or changing it protects nothing. Only encryption protects the traffic.
Device addresses are sent in the clear and can be copied, and the traffic is still protected only by WEP, which can be broken.

questions.prompt: A scan of a shop's web server shows these open ports. Which should be reachable from the whole internet, and which should be closed or limited to trusted addresses?
hints: Ask who actually needs to reach each service, and whether that is everyone.
Every open port that visitors do not need adds attack surface without adding to the website.

bins.label: Closed or limited to trusted addresses

items.label: 80/tcp http, the shop's website
items.explanation: Visitors reach the shop on this port.

items.label: 443/tcp https, the shop's website
items.explanation: Visitors reach the shop on this port, with encryption.

items.label: 22/tcp ssh, used by the administrators
items.explanation: It gives remote command access, so it belongs to the office addresses only.

items.label: 3306/tcp mysql, the shop's database
items.explanation: Only the web server needs to reach the database.

items.label: 3389/tcp remote desktop
items.explanation: It gives remote control of the machine and is a favourite target.

items.label: 445/tcp Windows file sharing
items.explanation: Nobody on the internet has a reason to browse the server's files.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Ports 80 and 443 serve the website to everyone, while ssh, the database, remote desktop and file sharing should be closed or limited to trusted addresses.

questions.onCorrect: Closing or limiting the surplus ports shrinks the attack surface without touching the website.

questions.prompt: Rules in order: 1 allow tcp 80 from any to web; 2 deny tcp 80 from 203.0.113.7 to web; 3 deny all. What happens to a packet from 203.0.113.7 to web on tcp 80?
hints: Rule 1 is checked first. Does it match this packet?
The firewall stops at the first rule that matches. Would rule 2 ever be consulted?
questions.onCorrect: Rule 1 matches any source, so rule 2 is never reached. The block on that address has to come above the general allow.

acceptedIdeas: It is allowed, since rule 1 matches it first
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is allowed, since rule 1 matches it first

choices.label: It is allowed, since rule 1 matches it first
It is denied, since rule 2 names this address
It is denied, since rule 3 denies everything left over

misconceptions.feedback: Rule 2 would deny it, but the firewall stops at the first rule that matches, and the allow rule above it matches a packet from any source.
Rule 3 is reached only by packets that no earlier rule matched, and this one is matched by the allow rule at the top.

questions.prompt: A firewall's rules read: 1 deny tcp 3389 from any to any; 2 allow all. The team then starts a database on tcp 5432. Who can reach it?
hints: Read the rules from the top and ask which one first matches a packet for port 5432.
Rule 1 is about port 3389 only.
questions.onCorrect: A list that ends in allow all turns every forgotten rule into an exposure that nobody notices. Ending in deny all turns it into an outage that someone fixes.

choices.label: Nobody, because no rule names port 5432 yet
Only hosts inside the network, because databases are internal by default
Everyone, because rule 2 allows whatever rule 1 does not name

acceptedIdeas: Everyone, because rule 2 allows whatever rule 1 does not name
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Everyone, because rule 2 allows whatever rule 1 does not name

misconceptions.feedback: A list that ends in allow all lets through everything not named above it. The missing rule leaves the door open.
The firewall knows nothing about what a service is. It decides by the rules, and neither rule mentions the inside of the network.

questions.prompt: A table `users` has 3 rows, and a program builds this query: `SELECT name FROM users WHERE name = '' OR '1'='1';` Roughly what does it return?
hints: Look at what comes after `OR`.
Ask whether `'1'='1'` depends on which row is being tested.
questions.onCorrect: The comparison `'1'='1'` is true for every row, so all 3 rows come back.

choices.label: An error, because the quotes do not pair up
Every row in the table
No rows, since no user has an empty name

acceptedIdeas: Every row in the table
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Every row in the table

misconceptions.feedback: No row has an empty name, but the condition goes on with `OR '1'='1'`, which is true whichever row is tested, so every row matches.
Every quote in this query has a partner, in `''` and in `'1'='1'`, so the database parses it without complaint.

questions.prompt: A login query reads `WHERE name = 'Ada' AND password = '' OR '1'='1'`. How does the database evaluate the condition?
hints: In arithmetic, multiplication is worked out before addition. SQL treats one of these two operators in the same way.
Ask which operator binds more tightly, and group the terms around it first.
questions.onCorrect: `AND` binds more tightly than `OR`, so the condition is true for every row, and the 4 rows of the table come back.

choices.label: It works out `AND` first, so `OR '1'='1'` makes every row match
It works out `OR` first, so only Ada's row can match
It refuses the query, because `AND` and `OR` cannot share a condition

acceptedIdeas: It works out `AND` first, so `OR '1'='1'` makes every row match
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It works out `AND` first, so `OR '1'='1'` makes every row match

misconceptions.feedback: SQL works out `AND` before `OR`, so the `OR` stands apart from the name test, and it is true for every row.
SQL accepts a condition with both operators and applies a fixed order between them.

questions.prompt: The login query is sent with markers and the typed text `' OR '1'='1` arrives as the password. The table has 4 users. What does the query return?
hints: The database compares the typed text letter by letter with each stored password.
The quotes and the word `OR` are now only characters in a text value.
questions.onCorrect: The login fails safely: the database was asked for a user with that odd password, and none exists.

choices.label: No rows, since no stored password equals that whole text
All 4 rows, since the extra condition is true for every user
Ada's row, since the name matched

acceptedIdeas: No rows, since no stored password equals that whole text
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No rows, since no stored password equals that whole text

misconceptions.feedback: That happens when the text is joined into the query. As a parameter it is only a value to compare, and it adds no condition.
Both parts of the condition still have to hold. The password must equal the typed text, and none does.

questions.prompt: A visitor's comment is `a<b`, and the page applies HTML encoding before inserting it. What text goes into the page's HTML?
hints: Encoding changes only the characters that mean something to HTML.
Ask which character in `a<b` has a meaning in HTML, and how the lesson said it is written.
questions.onCorrect: The browser displays `<` as a less-than sign, so the reader sees `a<b` as typed while the page's structure stays as the site wrote it.

choices.label: `a<b`
`ab`
`a<b`

acceptedIdeas: `a<b`
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: `a<b`

misconceptions.feedback: Inserting `a<b` unchanged lets the browser read `<` as the start of a tag, which is the fault that encoding exists to prevent.
Encoding keeps every character the visitor typed and changes only how `<` is written, so the reader still sees `a<b` on the page.
`%3C` is how `<` is written in a URL. Text placed in the body of an HTML page needs the HTML form, `<`, which is why the encoding has to suit the place where the text lands.

questions.prompt: A search page prints 'You searched for' followed by the search text taken from the address, without encoding it. A victim follows a link that carries a script in the search text. Which kind of cross-site scripting is this?
hints: Ask whether the script is kept anywhere, or arrives with the request.
Who is affected: everyone who visits the page, or the people sent the crafted link?
questions.onCorrect: Reflected XSS bounces off one request, so its victims are the people sent the crafted link, and the fix is the same encoding.

choices.label: Stored, because the page keeps the search text for later visitors
Reflected, because the script comes back in the response to the same request
Neither, because the script runs in the visitor's browser and not on the server

acceptedIdeas: Reflected, because the script comes back in the response to the same request
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Reflected, because the script comes back in the response to the same request

misconceptions.feedback: A stored attack is saved on the server and sent to every later visitor. Here the script travels in the link and in one request, and nothing is kept.
Both kinds run in the visitor's browser. The difference is whether the script is saved on the server or bounced off one request.

questions.prompt: A handler runs `"SELECT id, total FROM orders WHERE customer = '" + name + "'"`, where `name` comes from a form. With `name` set to `' OR '1'='1`, it returns all 5 rows of the table instead of the visitor's own. Which change closes the flaw?
hints: The fault is in building one string from the program's query and the visitor's input.
Which choice keeps the typed value out of the query's text altogether?
questions.onCorrect: With a parameter the query is parsed before the value arrives, so the quotes in the value are only characters to compare.

choices.label: Send the query as `... WHERE customer = ?` and pass `name` as a parameter
Strip the words `OR` and `AND` out of `name` before building the whole query
Double every quote in `name` before joining it into the query text
Check in the page's JavaScript that the form field holds no quote

acceptedIdeas: Send the query as `... WHERE customer = ?` and pass `name` as a parameter
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Send the query as `... WHERE customer = ?` and pass `name` as a parameter

misconceptions.feedback: A list of banned words is always incomplete, because the query has other keywords and spellings that do the same work.
Escaping by hand has to cover every special character in every context, and OWASP calls it error-prone and strongly discouraged in place of parameters.
The check runs in the visitor's browser, so anyone who sends the request without the page skips it. The server has to protect itself.

questions.prompt: An API sorts products with `?sort=price` and builds `"SELECT * FROM products ORDER BY " + sort`. A parameter marker can bind a value but not a column name. What closes the flaw?
hints: OWASP says that parameter markers represent data values, not table names, column names or keywords.
What can the server list in advance when only a few columns are allowed to be sorted?
questions.onCorrect: The allowed values are decided by the application and the caller only chooses among them, so nothing typed becomes part of the query.

choices.label: Allow only column names from a fixed list and reject the rest
Pass `sort` as a parameter, as for any other value in a query
Remove the quote characters from `sort` before it is joined in
Hide the sort option from the page so that callers cannot see it

acceptedIdeas: Allow only column names from a fixed list and reject the rest
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Allow only column names from a fixed list and reject the rest

misconceptions.feedback: A marker stands for a value. In `ORDER BY ?` the database sorts by the constant it was given, so the order does not change, and the sort never works.
Injection into a column position needs no quotes at all, so removing them does not decide whether the text is read as code.
A caller can send any `sort` value without a page that offers it. Hiding an option is not a check.

questions.prompt: A team finds six places where input reaches code. Which defence closes each one?
hints: Ask whether the untrusted input lands in a database query as a value, in a web page, or in a part of a query that cannot be a value.
A column name or a sort direction cannot be sent as a parameter.

items.label: A login query joined from the name and password boxes
items.explanation: The values travel apart from the query text, so they stay data.

items.label: A search page that prints the typed search text in its heading
items.explanation: The text is encoded for HTML so the browser shows it and never reads it as markup.

items.label: A report page that takes the column to sort by from the address
items.explanation: A column name cannot be a parameter, so only names on a fixed list are accepted.

items.label: A comment page that inserts each saved comment into its HTML
items.explanation: Encoding at the point of output works whatever the comment contains.

items.label: A lookup that selects a customer by a typed name
items.explanation: The name is a value, which a parameter keeps apart from the query.

items.label: An export that lets the user pick ascending or descending order
items.explanation: Only the literal words ASC and DESC are accepted, whatever was typed.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
