answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The login query and the customer lookup need parameters, the search heading and the comment page need output encoding, and the sort column and the order direction need an allow-list.

questions.onCorrect: The defence follows where the input lands: values go in parameters, text for a page is encoded, and structure is chosen from a fixed list.

questions.prompt: A correct server checks ownership on every request. Four requests arrive: (1) user 3 asks for invoice 310, which is theirs; (2) user 3 asks for invoice 311, which belongs to user 4; (3) user 4 asks for invoice 311; (4) user 3 asks for invoice 312, which belongs to user 8. Which requests does it deny?
hints: For each request, compare the signed-in user with the owner of the invoice.
Being signed in is not the same as being the owner. Which requests ask for someone else's invoice?
questions.onCorrect: Each decision compares the invoice's owner with the user asking, so the server needs no list of forbidden requests, only the owner of each object.

choices.label: Only request 2
Requests 2, 3 and 4
Requests 2 and 4
None, since every user is signed in

acceptedIdeas: Requests 2 and 4
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Requests 2 and 4

misconceptions.feedback: Request 4 also asks for an invoice that belongs to someone else, user 8, so it fails the same check as request 2.
Invoice 311 belongs to user 4, so request 3 is the owner asking for their own invoice and is allowed.
Signing in shows who each user is but not which invoices they may see, and the server has to check that on each request.

questions.prompt: A site changes data only through POST requests, sets its session cookie to allow cross-site sending, and has no token. Can a hidden form on another site still send a request that carries the cookie?
hints: Ask what a page on another site is able to submit, and what the browser then attaches to it.
The method of a request is chosen by whoever writes the form.
questions.onCorrect: The method makes no difference to whether the cookie is attached, so a token or a SameSite cookie is needed.

choices.label: No, since a page on another site can send only GET requests
No, since browsers never attach a site's cookies to requests that start elsewhere
Yes, since a hidden form can submit a POST and the browser attaches the cookie

acceptedIdeas: Yes, since a hidden form can submit a POST and the browser attaches the cookie
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Yes, since a hidden form can submit a POST and the browser attaches the cookie

misconceptions.feedback: An HTML form can use the POST method, and a hidden one can be submitted by script, so POST is no barrier.
Browsers attach a site's cookies to requests to that site unless the cookie's SameSite setting withholds them, and this cookie allows cross-site sending.

questions.prompt: Which cookie attribute tells the browser not to attach the cookie to requests that begin on another site?
hints: The attribute controls whether the cookie travels with requests that start on another site.
Its name says that the cookie is kept to the same site.
questions.onCorrect: Strict withholds the cookie from every cross-site request, and Lax withholds it from most of them, including form posts.

acceptedIdeas: SameSite
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: SameSite

questions.prompt: A site hides the link to `/admin/users` from ordinary users' menus, but a user who types the address into the browser sees the page. What is the flaw?
hints: Ask where the check for `/admin/users` happens: in the menu or in the server.
A user who types an address skips every menu. What stops them then?
questions.onCorrect: Hiding the link changes only what the browser shows, and the authorisation check has to be in the server.

acceptedIdeas: Broken access control
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Broken access control

choices.label: Cross-site request forgery
Server-side request forgery
Broken access control
Cross-site scripting

misconceptions.feedback: A forged request is sent by another site, using the user's cookie. Here the user types the address personally.
Server-side forgery needs the server to fetch an address on a visitor's behalf, and nothing here makes the server fetch anything.
No script is put into a page. The user simply asks for an address that the server should have refused.

questions.prompt: A mobile app's API serves orders at `/api/orders/` followed by a random 128-bit identifier that cannot be guessed. A user obtains someone else's identifier from a forwarded email and requests that order. Must the server still check that the order belongs to the user?
hints: Ask what the server does with a valid identifier that comes from someone who does not own the order.
Think about how an identifier can leak: a forwarded email, a log, the browser history.
questions.onCorrect: Obscurity only makes an identifier hard to find, and anyone who learns it, from a link or a log, would be let in without the check.

choices.label: Yes, since anyone who learns the identifier would otherwise be let in
No, since the link must have been shared on purpose by the order's owner
No, since an identifier that cannot be guessed is protection enough

acceptedIdeas: Yes, since anyone who learns the identifier would otherwise be let in
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Yes, since anyone who learns the identifier would otherwise be let in

misconceptions.feedback: The identifier cannot be guessed, but this user did not guess it: they read it in a forwarded email, so being hard to guess has not kept it secret.
The email was forwarded, so nobody chose to give this user the order, and a link can reach people its owner never meant it to.

questions.prompt: A feature fetches an image from a link that the user types, and it refuses the addresses 127.0.0.1 and 169.254.169.254. An attacker gives it a link to a site of their own, which redirects to 169.254.169.254. Which control would have stopped the request?
hints: Think about which list has to be right about a short set of hosts, and which about every bad address there could be.
An attacker controls where a redirect leads. Can a list of bad addresses name them all?
questions.onCorrect: A short list of the destinations the feature needs leaves no room for spellings and redirects that a blocklist would miss.

choices.label: A longer blocklist that names more spellings of internal addresses
A check that the response is an image before it is returned
An allowlist of the hosts that the feature needs

acceptedIdeas: An allowlist of the hosts that the feature needs
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: An allowlist of the hosts that the feature needs

misconceptions.feedback: A blocklist has to anticipate every spelling and every redirect, and a longer one leaves the same gap: the link here looks harmless until the redirect.
The request reaches its target whatever the response turns out to be, so checking the response afterwards is too late.

questions.prompt: A shop's log shows `user=7 GET /invoices/1040 200`, `user=7 GET /invoices/1041 200`, `user=7 GET /invoices/1042 200` and `user=7 GET /invoices/1043 200`. User 7 owns only invoice 1040. What does the log show?
hints: User 7 owns invoice 1040 only. What does the status on 1041, 1042 and 1043 tell you?
Ask what the server compared before it answered each request.
questions.onCorrect: The server answers every identifier without comparing the invoice's owner with the signed-in user, so one account can read the others.

choices.label: Normal browsing, since a 200 status means the requests were allowed
Cross-site request forgery, since the requests came from another website
User 7 reading others' invoices, since the server does not check owners
SQL injection, since the identifier in the path keeps changing

acceptedIdeas: User 7 reading others' invoices, since the server does not check owners
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: User 7 reading others' invoices, since the server does not check owners

misconceptions.feedback: A 200 status means the server answered. It says nothing about whether the user was entitled to the answer.
A forged request would come from a page on another site. These requests are made by user 7, one after another.
Changing a number in the path is not injection. The numbers are valid identifiers, and the server hands over whatever they name.

questions.prompt: A team reviews six defences. Which flaw does each one answer?
hints: Ask who makes the unwanted request: a signed-in user, the user's browser on another site's instructions, or the server itself.
A check on the server about which object a user may reach belongs to access control.

items.label: Compare the invoice's owner with the signed-in user on every request
items.explanation: The server decides, for each object, whether this user may have it.

items.label: Mark the session cookie SameSite so other sites cannot make it travel
items.explanation: The browser stops attaching the cookie to requests that start elsewhere.

items.label: Match the destination host against a list of the hosts the feature needs
items.explanation: The server only fetches addresses that it was meant to fetch.

items.label: Check the user's role on the server before serving `/admin/users`
items.explanation: Hiding the link decides nothing. The check belongs in the server's code.

items.label: Require a random token in each form that another site cannot read
items.explanation: A forged request cannot include a value it cannot see.

items.label: Turn off redirect following in the code that fetches the address
items.explanation: A redirect could send an approved address on to an internal one.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The owner comparison and the role check answer broken access control, the SameSite cookie and the form token answer request forgery from another site, and the host list and the redirect switch answer server-side request forgery.

questions.onCorrect: Each defence sits where the unwanted request is made: at the object, in the browser's cookie handling, or in the server's own fetching code.

questions.prompt: A photo-import feature fetches the address a user types. A tester gives it `http://localhost:8080/admin`, and the page that comes back is the server's private admin page. What kind of flaw is this?
hints: Ask who made the request to the admin page: the tester's browser, or the server?
The server sits inside the network and often reaches things that the user cannot.
questions.onCorrect: The server made a request on behalf of the visitor, so the check belongs in its outbound code, which compares the destination with an allowlist.

choices.label: Cross-site request forgery, because a request was made without the user meaning it
Server-side request forgery, because the server fetched an address it was handed
Cross-site scripting, because a page showed content that the tester supplied
Insecure direct object reference, because an identifier was changed

acceptedIdeas: Server-side request forgery, because the server fetched an address it was handed
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Server-side request forgery, because the server fetched an address it was handed

misconceptions.feedback: Request forgery across sites makes a victim's browser send a request. Here the server itself made the request.
No script ran in a browser. The server fetched a page and returned it.
No identifier of a stored object was changed. The input was an address that the server went and fetched.

questions.prompt: Which policy gives an attacker the larger search space: 6 random characters from the 62 letters and digits, or 8 random lowercase letters?
hints: The search space is the alphabet size multiplied by itself once for each position.
Work out 62 to the 6th and 26 to the 8th, and compare them.
questions.onCorrect: 26^8 is 208,827,064,576 and 62^6 is 56,800,235,584, so length can beat alphabet size.

choices.label: 8 lowercase letters, about 209 billion against about 57 billion
6 characters from 62, since a bigger alphabet always gives the larger space
They are equal, since both are random characters

acceptedIdeas: 8 lowercase letters, about 209 billion against about 57 billion
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 8 lowercase letters, about 209 billion against about 57 billion

misconceptions.feedback: Each extra position multiplies the space by the alphabet size. Two more positions from 26 outweigh the larger alphabet over six.
Random does not make them equal. The count is the alphabet size raised to the length, which differs between the two.

questions.prompt: A password is made of random characters, each one of the 62 letters and digits. One more random character is added. Roughly what happens to the number of possible passwords?
hints: Each position can be filled in 62 ways, independently of the others.
Ask what the new position multiplies the count by, and not what it adds.
questions.onCorrect: This is why length counts for so much: each character multiplies the work, and widening the alphabet raises the base only once.

choices.label: It doubles
It becomes 62 times as large
It grows a little, by 62 more passwords

acceptedIdeas: It becomes 62 times as large
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It becomes 62 times as large

misconceptions.feedback: Each existing password can be followed by any of the 62 symbols, so every one of them becomes 62 passwords, not one more.
Doubling would be right for a position with two choices. Here the new position has 62 choices, so the count is multiplied by 62.

questions.prompt: What does a ninth character, from the same alphabet of 36 symbols, do to the number of candidates?
hints: Each position can be filled in 36 ways, independently of the others.
Ask what the new position multiplies the count by, and not what it adds.
questions.onCorrect: The factor is the alphabet size each time, so ten characters have 36 times as many candidates as nine.

choices.label: It multiplies the number by 36.
It adds 36 more candidates to the count.
It doubles the number.

acceptedIdeas: It multiplies the number by 36.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It multiplies the number by 36.

misconceptions.feedback: Adding 36 would be tiny beside 2.8 trillion. Each existing candidate can be followed by any of 36 symbols, so the count is multiplied.
Doubling would add one bit. A symbol drawn from 36 possibilities multiplies the count by 36.

questions.prompt: How many hours does a full search of 36^10 = 3,656,158,440,062,976 candidates take at 10 billion guesses a second? Give the answer to two decimal places.
hints: Divide the number of candidates by the guesses per second to get seconds.
Divide the seconds by 3,600 to get hours.
The seconds come to about 365,616.
questions.onCorrect: One more character lengthened the search from under 3 hours to over 4 days.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the time in seconds. Divide by 3,600 to give hours.
That divides by 60 only, which gives minutes. Divide by 3,600 for hours.

questions.prompt: A scanner reads the pattern of veins in the palm of the user's hand, and a site accepts the result as evidence of identity. Which kind of factor is the palm scan?
hints: Think about whether the scanner reads something you know, something you hold, or something about your body.
A palm pattern cannot be changed after it leaks.
questions.onCorrect: A palm pattern cannot be changed if it leaks, so it works best combined with a factor of another kind.

choices.label: Something you know
Something you have
Something you are

acceptedIdeas: Something you are
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Something you are

misconceptions.feedback: The scanner that reads the palm is something you have, but the pattern of veins is part of your body.
A palm pattern is not a secret that you remember, and you cannot choose or change it.

questions.prompt: A site's leaked user table holds `alice 5f4dcc3b5aa765d61d8327deb882cf99`, `bob 5f4dcc3b5aa765d61d8327deb882cf99` and `carol 482c811da5d5b4bc6d497ffa98491e38`. They are MD5 digests with no salt. What can an attacker who has stolen the table do?
hints: Look at the digests of alice and bob. What does it tell you about their passwords?
Without a salt, hashing a guess gives the same value for every account that chose it.
questions.onCorrect: An unsalted fast hash gives away which users share a password and lets one search cover the whole table. A salt and a slow hash take both away.

choices.label: Nothing, since a digest cannot be turned back into the password
Crack the accounts one at a time, since each one needs its own separate search
See that Alice and Bob share a password, and test guesses against all three

acceptedIdeas: See that Alice and Bob share a password, and test guesses against all three
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: See that Alice and Bob share a password, and test guesses against all three

misconceptions.feedback: A digest cannot be reversed, but it can be guessed at. An attacker hashes candidate passwords and compares, and a fast hash lets them try billions a second.
With no salt, one guess hashed once is compared with every account, so one search covers all of them.

questions.prompt: A site requires passwords of at least 8 characters with a capital, a digit and a symbol, and makes everyone change theirs every 60 days. What does NIST SP 800-63B advise instead?
hints: NIST asks what a rule does to the passwords that people actually pick.
Which one of the three checks does NIST require verifiers to make against a list?
questions.onCorrect: NIST keeps a length minimum, checks new passwords against lists of common and breached ones, and asks for a change only when there is evidence of compromise.

choices.label: Keep both rules, because mixed characters and frequent changes slow guessing
Drop the character rules and forced changes, and block common passwords
Drop the length minimum, because the composition rules already do the work

acceptedIdeas: Drop the character rules and forced changes, and block common passwords
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Drop the character rules and forced changes, and block common passwords

misconceptions.feedback: NIST says verifiers should not impose other composition rules and should not require arbitrary changes. People answer both with predictable patterns.
NIST keeps a minimum length for user-chosen passwords and asks verifiers to accept long ones. The composition rules are what it advises against.

questions.prompt: A site accepts any password of exactly 7 characters from the 62 letters and digits. An attacker with a copy of the hashes can try 10 billion guesses a second. About how many minutes does it take to try every possible password? Give the answer to one decimal place.
hints: Find the number of passwords first: 62 choices for each of 7 positions.
Divide by the guesses per second, then change seconds to minutes.
The count is about 3.5 trillion and the rate is 10 billion a second.
questions.onCorrect: Seven characters fall in under six minutes at that speed, and each further character multiplies the time by 62.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: There are 62^7 = 3,521,614,606,208 passwords. Divided by 10,000,000,000 a second that is 352.16 seconds, and 352.16 / 60 = 5.87, which is 5.9 minutes.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the time in seconds. The question asks for minutes.
That is the time in hours. Multiply by 60 to get minutes.

questions.prompt: A rule says that only the author of a document may delete it. Which kind of model fits the rule better?
hints: Ask what the rule compares: the user's role, or the user and the particular document.
A role is the same for every document. The author of each document is not.
questions.onCorrect: No role can say "author of this document" without one role per document, while an attribute comparison states it directly.

choices.label: Role-based, by giving every writer an author role
Role-based, with a separate role for the author of every document
Attribute-based, by comparing the user with the document's author

acceptedIdeas: Attribute-based, by comparing the user with the document's author
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Attribute-based, by comparing the user with the document's author

misconceptions.feedback: An author role would let every writer delete every document, including other people's, since a role cannot say whose document it is.
A role for each document would multiply roles with every new document, which is the problem that attributes were brought in to solve.

questions.prompt: A cross-site scripting flaw lets a script run in the page and try to read `document.cookie`. Which cookie attribute stops page scripts from reading the session cookie?
hints: The attribute has to do with who may read the cookie, not with where it is sent.
One attribute tells the browser to keep the cookie from scripts altogether.
questions.onCorrect: `HttpOnly` stops scripts reading the cookie. A flaw that runs a script can still act as the user, but cannot carry the identifier away.

choices.label: HttpOnly
Secure
SameSite=Strict
Path=/

acceptedIdeas: HttpOnly
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: HttpOnly

misconceptions.feedback: `Secure` keeps the cookie off unencrypted connections. A script on the page can still read it.
`SameSite` limits which requests carry the cookie. It does not hide the cookie from scripts in the page.
`Path` sets which parts of the site receive the cookie. Scripts on those pages can still read it.

questions.prompt: A user lets a calendar app read the contacts they keep with an email provider, using OAuth. Which of the four OAuth parties is the calendar app?
hints: Ask which party wants something done with the contacts, and which holds them.
The app asks for access on the user's behalf.
questions.onCorrect: The calendar app is the client: the application that wants access and receives the tokens.

choices.label: The client
The resource owner
The authorisation server
The resource server

acceptedIdeas: The client
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The client

misconceptions.feedback: The resource owner is the user, who grants the access.
The authorisation server is the email provider's sign-in service, which issues the tokens.
The resource server holds the contacts and accepts the access token.

questions.prompt: A user clicks Log out, and the site only deletes the session cookie in the browser. The server still accepts that session identifier. A copy of the cookie was stolen earlier. What can the thief do?
hints: Where does the server look up who is signed in?
What did the logout change on the server?
questions.onCorrect: OWASP requires the server to invalidate the session at logout, because clearing the cookie in the browser does not stop another copy being used.

choices.label: Keep using the account, since the server never cancelled the session
Nothing at all, since the user has logged out and the cookie was deleted
Read pages already open, but not make any new request on the account

acceptedIdeas: Keep using the account, since the server never cancelled the session
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Keep using the account, since the server never cancelled the session

misconceptions.feedback: The server decides who is signed in, and it still holds the session. Deleting the cookie from one browser changes nothing there.
Whoever sends the identifier is treated as the user for new requests too, until the server ends the session.

questions.prompt: The `shop-api` receives a token with a valid signature whose payload reads `{"iss":"https://login.example","aud":"billing-api","sub":"ana","exp":1893456000}`. The time is 1893454200 seconds. What should `shop-api` do?
hints: List the checks a receiver makes: signature, issuer, audience, expiry.
Compare the audience claim with the name of the service that received the token.
questions.onCorrect: A token made for one service should not be accepted by another, which is why the audience is checked as well as the signature.

choices.label: Accept it, since the signature is valid and the token has not expired
Reject it, since the audience names another service
Accept it, since the issuer is the login service it trusts

acceptedIdeas: Reject it, since the audience names another service
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Reject it, since the audience names another service

misconceptions.feedback: Both checks pass, but the token was made for `billing-api`. Accepting it would let a token for one service open another.
The issuer matches, but the audience does not. Every claim has to be checked, the audience included.

questions.prompt: A user lets a photo-printing service read the pictures they keep with another company, using OAuth. Which OAuth party signs the user in and issues the tokens?
hints: There are four parties: the user, the app that wants access, the server that holds the pictures, and one more.
Which party checks who the user is and decides what to hand out?
questions.onCorrect: The authorisation server signs the user in and issues the tokens, and the resource server accepts them.

acceptedIdeas: authorisation server
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: authorisation server

misconceptions.feedback: The client is the app asking for access, which here is the printing service. It receives the tokens and does not issue them.
The resource server holds the pictures and accepts the access token. The party that signs the user in and issues it is a different one.
The resource owner is the user, who grants the access. A different party signs the user in and issues the tokens.

questions.prompt: A message was enciphered with a Caesar shift of 3 and reads WKUHDW. Shift each letter back by 3. What is the plain word?
hints: Count three places back in the alphabet from each letter, and wrap round at A.
Check your word by shifting it forward by 3. It should give back the message.
questions.onCorrect: Decrypting reverses the shift with the same key, which is why the key must stay secret even when the method is known.

acceptedIdeas: THREAT
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: THREAT

misconceptions.feedback: That shifts each letter forward by 3, which is how the message was made. Decrypting moves each letter back.

questions.prompt: A system's key grows from 40 bits to 41 bits. What happens to the time needed to try every possible key?
hints: A key of n bits can take 2^n values.
Compare 2^41 with 2^40.
questions.onCorrect: Each extra bit doubles the key space, so 128 bits has 2^88 times as many keys as 40 bits.

choices.label: It rises by about 2.5%, one part in forty
It is unchanged, since only the length changed
It doubles

acceptedIdeas: It doubles
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It doubles

misconceptions.feedback: The key space is 2 raised to the number of bits, so one more bit multiplies it by 2 and does not add a fortieth.
The number of keys is 2 raised to the length, so a longer key has more of them.

questions.prompt: In Python, a program computes `cipher = 11 ^ 6`, using 6 as the key. What does `cipher ^ 6` give?
hints: Write 11 as 1011 and 6 as 0110, and XOR them bit by bit.
XOR gives 1 where the bits differ. Apply the same key to the result.
questions.onCorrect: 11 ^ 6 is 13, and 13 ^ 6 is 11. XOR with the same key twice returns the original, which is why one function can both encrypt and decrypt.

choices.label: 13, the cipher value again
6, the key itself
11, the original number

acceptedIdeas: 11, the original number
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 11, the original number

misconceptions.feedback: 13 is `11 ^ 6`. Applying the same key a second time undoes the first step.
Applying the key twice cancels it out and leaves the original number, not the key.

questions.prompt: A team hashes an invoice file with SHA-256 on Monday and again on Friday. The two 64-character digests differ in almost every character. What does that show?
hints: The same input always gives the same digest.
Think about what a change of a single character does to the digest.
questions.onCorrect: A mismatch means the bytes differ. The digests of `invoice 100 paid` and `invoice 101 paid` share almost nothing, although the inputs differ by one character.

choices.label: SHA-256 adds a random value each time, so digests of one file always differ
The file changed in between, since one input always gives the same digest
Only a few characters of the file changed, because the digests differ where it did

acceptedIdeas: The file changed in between, since one input always gives the same digest
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The file changed in between, since one input always gives the same digest

misconceptions.feedback: A hash has no random input. Hashing the same file always gives the same digest, and a salt is what makes stored password hashes differ.
A tiny change to the input gives a completely different digest, so a large difference in the digest says nothing about how much of the file changed.

questions.prompt: Which key does the vendor use to sign its update?
hints: Think about who must be able to produce a valid signature, and who must be able to check one.
One key is kept secret by the vendor and one is given to everybody.
questions.onCorrect: Anyone can check the signature with the public key, but only the holder of the private key can produce one.

acceptedIdeas: The private key, which only the vendor holds
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The private key, which only the vendor holds

choices.label: The public key, which the vendor gives to every user
A shared key that the vendor and every user hold
The private key, which only the vendor holds

misconceptions.feedback: Everyone holds the public key, so a signature made with it would say nothing about who made it. Users use it to check a signature.
If every user holds the key, any of them could make a valid signature, so it would not show that the update came from the vendor.

questions.prompt: A site stores customers' passwords as base64 text and calls them encrypted. Does base64 protect the passwords from someone who steals the database?
hints: Ask whether base64 needs a key to be undone.
The lesson called base64 an encoding. What is the difference between an encoding and encryption?
questions.onCorrect: Base64 rewrites bytes as text, and anyone can reverse it, so it is an encoding and not encryption.

choices.label: No, since base64 uses no key and anyone can reverse it
Yes, provided the thief does not know which encoding was used
Yes, since base64 text cannot be read by eye

acceptedIdeas: No, since base64 uses no key and anyone can reverse it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No, since base64 uses no key and anyone can reverse it

misconceptions.feedback: Base64 looks scrambled to a person, but any program reverses it in an instant, since it only rewrites bytes as letters and digits.
By Kerckhoffs's principle the method must be assumed known, and base64 is recognisable at a glance, so hiding the choice protects nothing.

questions.prompt: A team lists eight needs. Which primitive fits each one?
hints: Ask who must be able to produce the result, and who must be able to check it.
A keyless fingerprint cannot tell you who made something. A key can.

items.label: Check that a downloaded installer matches the digest on the publisher's page
items.explanation: A hash is a keyless fingerprint that shows whether the bytes changed.

items.label: Fingerprint a stored document so that a later copy can be compared with it
items.explanation: The same input always gives the same digest, and a small change gives a different one.

items.label: Keep a backup file secret from someone who steals the disk
items.explanation: Secrecy between parties who hold the same key calls for symmetric encryption.

items.label: Protect the bulk of the data in a TLS connection after the handshake
items.explanation: Symmetric encryption is fast, and the handshake supplies the shared key.

items.label: Let customers confirm that an update came from the vendor
items.explanation: Only the vendor's private key makes a valid mark, and anyone can check it with the public key.

items.label: Let anyone check that a signed contract came from its sender
items.explanation: The sender's private key signs and the public key verifies.

items.label: Let two services that share a key detect requests forged by an outsider
items.explanation: A message authentication code needs the shared key, which the outsider lacks.

items.label: Stop a client from editing a cookie value that only the server may set
items.explanation: The server keys the value, so an edit by anyone without the key is detected.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The installer check and the stored fingerprint use a hash, the backup file and the TLS data use symmetric encryption, the update and the contract use a digital signature, and the two services and the cookie use a message authentication code.

questions.onCorrect: Each primitive answers a different question: a hash shows change, symmetric encryption keeps secrets, a signature shows who made something, and a code shows that someone with the key did.

questions.prompt: A startup designs its own cipher for customer messages and keeps the design secret, saying that nobody can break what they cannot see. What is the best reply?
hints: Ask which part of the scheme can be replaced if it leaks: the key or the design.
Algorithms such as AES were chosen after years of open attack by researchers.
questions.onCorrect: A published, reviewed algorithm puts all of the secrecy in the key, which can be changed if it leaks.

choices.label: Use a published algorithm such as AES, so that only the key stays secret
Keep the design secret, and make the key longer to make up for any weakness
Use AES with each block encrypted on its own, since that is the simplest way

acceptedIdeas: Use a published algorithm such as AES, so that only the key stays secret
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Use a published algorithm such as AES, so that only the key stays secret

misconceptions.feedback: A design that has had no outside examination may fail however long its key is, and a secret algorithm cannot be changed once it leaks.
Encrypting each block on its own is ECB mode, which leaks patterns in the data. The mode matters as much as the algorithm.

questions.prompt: A legacy system encrypts with a 40-bit key, and an attacker can try 1 billion keys a second. About how many minutes does it take to try every key? Give the answer to one decimal place.
hints: The number of keys is 2 multiplied by itself 40 times.
Divide the number of keys by the guesses per second to get seconds.
About 1,100 seconds. How many minutes is that?
questions.onCorrect: A 40-bit key falls in under twenty minutes. A 128-bit key takes more than 10^22 years at the same speed.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: There are 2^40 = 1,099,511,627,776 keys. Divided by 1,000,000,000 a second that is 1,099.5 seconds, and 1,099.5 / 60 = 18.3 minutes.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the time in seconds. The question asks for minutes.

questions.prompt: During the handshake, the browser checks the server's signature with the public key in its certificate. What kind of cryptography is that?
hints: The client holds the certificate's public key and checks a signature made with the matching private key.
Does a signature use one shared key, or a pair of keys?
questions.onCorrect: Public-key operations are slow, so TLS uses them only to agree on keys and to prove identity, and then protects the data with a fast symmetric key.

acceptedIdeas: Asymmetric, since it works with a key pair
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Asymmetric, since it works with a key pair

choices.label: Asymmetric, since it works with a key pair
Hashing, since a signature is a fingerprint
Symmetric, since both sides use the same key

misconceptions.feedback: A hash is part of how a signature is made, but a hash has no key. Checking a signature needs the signer's public key.
A symmetric operation uses one key held by both sides. The browser holds only the public key, and the matching private key stays with the server.

questions.prompt: A browser trusts Root CA. A server presents a leaf certificate signed by Intermediate B, Intermediate B's certificate is signed by Intermediate A, and Intermediate A's certificate is signed by Root CA. Which signatures must the browser verify to trust the leaf?
hints: The browser starts from the one certificate it already trusts and works down the chain.
Each certificate in the chain must be signed by the one above it. How many signatures is that between the root and the leaf?
questions.onCorrect: Each link is a signature by the certificate above it, and the chain stops at the root because trusting the root is a decision already made.

choices.label: Only the leaf's signature, made by Intermediate B
The leaf's and both intermediates', signed by B, A and Root CA
All four, including the root's signature on its own certificate

acceptedIdeas: All four, including the root's signature on its own certificate
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: All four, including the root's signature on its own certificate

misconceptions.feedback: The leaf's signature shows only that Intermediate B vouched for it, and the browser has no reason to trust Intermediate B until it has followed the signatures up to Root CA.
Root CA is already in the trust store and its certificate is signed by itself, so checking that signature would prove nothing new.

questions.prompt: A server at `api.example.com` presents a certificate for `www.example.com`. Which check fails?
hints: Compare the name the browser asked for with the name in the certificate.
Which of the four checks looks at names?
questions.onCorrect: A certificate for one name is evidence about that name only, so a mismatch ends the connection.

choices.label: The dates the certificate is valid between
Whether the issuer has withdrawn the certificate
The chain of signatures up to a trusted root
The name the certificate was issued for

acceptedIdeas: The name the certificate was issued for
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The name the certificate was issued for

misconceptions.feedback: The dates could be fine. The fault lies in which name the certificate was issued for.
The signatures could all verify. The certificate is a valid statement about a different name.
Nothing says the certificate was withdrawn. The mismatch is between the site that was asked for and the one the certificate names.

questions.prompt: A certificate's name and chain are fine, and it expired three days ago. Why does the browser refuse the connection?
hints: The browser makes four checks. How many of them have to pass?
Which check is about today's date?
questions.onCorrect: The browser refuses the connection when any one of the four checks fails.

choices.label: Any one failed check stops the connection, and the dates check has failed
An expired certificate also fails the name check
Only a revoked certificate stops a connection, so this one must have been withdrawn

acceptedIdeas: Any one failed check stops the connection, and the dates check has failed
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Any one failed check stops the connection, and the dates check has failed

misconceptions.feedback: The name check compares the certificate's name with the site that was requested, and the dates play no part in it.
Revocation is a fourth, separate check. An expired certificate fails the dates check even if the issuer never withdrew it.

questions.prompt: A certificate is valid until 30 May 2026. How many days remain on 20 April 2026?
hints: Count the days remaining in April after the 20th.
Add the days of May up to the 30th.
The two parts are 10 and 30.
questions.onCorrect: A monitor that warns at 30 days would fire ten days from now, which is why many teams alert earlier still.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: There are 10 days left in April after the 20th and 30 days in May up to the 30th: 10 + 30 = 40.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only the days left in April. Add the days of May up to the 30th.
That counts only May. Add the days left in April after the 20th.

questions.prompt: A phishing page for a lookalike bank name has a valid certificate for its own name and shows the padlock. Does the padlock show that it is safe to type your bank password into it?
hints: Ask what the padlock says about the name in the address bar, and what it says about who owns the site.
The attacker can obtain a certificate for a name that the attacker owns.
questions.onCorrect: The padlock says that the connection is encrypted to the named site. Whether that site deserves trust is a different question.

choices.label: Yes, since browsers refuse certificates for lookalike names, so it must be real
No, since it shows only that the connection is encrypted to the name shown
Yes, since a certificate authority has vouched for the site and checked for fraud

acceptedIdeas: No, since it shows only that the connection is encrypted to the name shown
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No, since it shows only that the connection is encrypted to the name shown

misconceptions.feedback: The authority checked only that the applicant controls the lookalike name, which a criminal can register as easily as anyone.
A lookalike name is a different, valid name, and the browser checks only that the certificate matches the name in the address.

questions.prompt: What makes a client trust a certificate from a site it has never visited?
hints: Ask what the client already holds before it ever meets the site.
A signature is only worth what the client already trusts about whoever made it.
questions.onCorrect: The root is trusted because the client already holds it, and each signature extends that trust one link.

choices.label: The connection to the site is encrypted, so it must be genuine
The certificate is signed with the site's own private key, which only it holds
A chain of signatures leads to a root that the client already trusts
Many other visitors have accepted the same certificate

acceptedIdeas: A chain of signatures leads to a root that the client already trusts
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A chain of signatures leads to a root that the client already trusts

misconceptions.feedback: Encryption can protect a connection to an impostor as well as to the real site, so it says nothing about whose certificate this is.
Anyone can sign a certificate with their own key, so a signature by the site itself gives a client no reason to trust it.
How many visitors have accepted a certificate plays no part in the checks.

questions.prompt: A browser opens a TLS 1.3 connection to `shop.example.com`. In what order do these things happen?
hints: The secret cannot be computed until both halves of the key exchange have been sent.
The certificate is sent encrypted, so it must come after the keys exist.

items: The client sends a ClientHello with its half of a key exchange and the name of the site
The server answers with a ServerHello that chooses the algorithms and carries its own half
Both sides compute the same secret, which never crosses the network
The server sends its certificate and a signature over the handshake, now encrypted
The client checks the certificate and both sides send application data under the new keys

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The client's hello comes first, then the server's hello, then both sides compute the shared secret, then the server sends its encrypted certificate and signature, and then the data flows under the new keys.

questions.onCorrect: The keys are agreed from the first two messages, which is why everything after them can be encrypted.

questions.prompt: A browser refuses eight connections. Which of its four checks has failed in each?
hints: The four checks are the name, the dates, the chain and revocation. Which one does each fault break?
A missing intermediate and an unknown CA both stop the chain from reaching a trusted root.

items.label: A certificate for `shop.example` is presented at `pay.example`
items.explanation: The name in the certificate does not match the site that was asked for.

items.label: A certificate for `www.example.com` is presented at `api.example.com`
items.explanation: A certificate must list the exact name that was requested.

items.label: The certificate's last valid day was last Tuesday
items.explanation: Today falls outside the dates in the certificate.

items.label: The certificate's first valid day is next week
items.explanation: A certificate is not yet valid before its start date.

items.label: The chain ends at a private company CA that the browser does not list
items.explanation: The chain does not lead to a root in the trust store.

items.label: The server sends its own certificate and leaves out the intermediate
items.explanation: The browser cannot link the certificate to a trusted root.

items.label: The issuer withdrew the certificate after its private key leaked
items.explanation: The certificate was cancelled before its end date.

items.label: The issuer cancelled a certificate it had issued by mistake
items.explanation: The issuer withdrew it, so it can no longer be trusted.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The two wrong-name certificates fail the name check, the expired and not-yet-valid certificates fail the dates check, the unknown CA and the missing intermediate fail the chain check, and the two withdrawn certificates fail revocation.

questions.onCorrect: Each warning is one failed check, which tells you whether to look at the server's name, its dates, its chain or its issuer.

questions.prompt: Using the lesson's rule, which finding should be patched first: an 8.8 on an internal server with no attacks seen, or a 5.9 on an internet-facing server where attacks have been seen?
hints: Multiply each score by its weight: 3 for internet-facing, 2 for internal.
Add the 10 only where attacks have been seen.
questions.onCorrect: The 5.9 reaches 27.7 because the server is exposed and attackers are using the flaw, which is the order a team should work in.

choices.label: The 8.8, since the higher CVSS score always goes first
Either one, since both are above the 4.0 line
The 5.9, which scores 27.7 against 17.6 for the 8.8

acceptedIdeas: The 5.9, which scores 27.7 against 17.6 for the 8.8
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The 5.9, which scores 27.7 against 17.6 for the 8.8

misconceptions.feedback: A higher score does not always go first. The rule adds the exposure weight and the 10 for attacks seen.
The two findings come out at very different priorities under the rule, and one of them is already being attacked.

questions.prompt: Why does the rule give an internet-facing server a higher weight than an isolated one?
hints: Think about how many people can reach a server on the internet compared with an isolated one.
The weight stands for how likely an attempt is.
questions.onCorrect: Exposure raises the likelihood of an attempt, which is the part of risk that a technical score does not contain.

choices.label: More attackers can reach it, so an attempt is likelier
A successful attack on it does more damage to the business
The same flaw gets a higher CVSS score there

acceptedIdeas: More attackers can reach it, so an attempt is likelier
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: More attackers can reach it, so an attempt is likelier

misconceptions.feedback: Damage depends on what the server holds, and an internet-facing server may hold very little and still be attacked.
The score is the same for the same flaw wherever it sits. The weight accounts for what the score leaves out.

questions.prompt: A sixth finding, F, is a 6.4 on an internet-facing server, and attacks have been seen. Using the same rule, what is its priority?
hints: Multiply the score by the weight first.
Attacks have been seen, so add the extra 10 after that.
questions.onCorrect: Evidence of use can lift a middling score to the top of the list, and the list needs to be refreshed as that evidence arrives.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 6.4 × 3 = 19.2, and 19.2 + 10 = 29.2. Finding B scores 32.5, so F would come second.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the product before the extra 10 for exploitation is added.
That adds 10 to the score and leaves out the weight. The weight multiplies the score first.

questions.prompt: A team wants to find a known-vulnerable library in its project before release. Which check does this?
hints: Ask what the check has to look at: your own code, a list of components, or files that hold keys.
The flaw is in someone else's library that the project includes.
questions.onCorrect: A dependency scan works from a list of the libraries and their versions, which is why a software bill of materials helps.

choices.label: Dependency scanning
Secret scanning of the repository
Static analysis of the source code

acceptedIdeas: Dependency scanning
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Dependency scanning

misconceptions.feedback: Static analysis reads the team's own source for dangerous patterns, and it does not compare the libraries with a database of known flaws.
Secret scanning looks for passwords and keys committed by mistake, not for flawed libraries.

questions.prompt: A scanner reports no findings on an application. Does that show that the application has no vulnerabilities?
hints: Ask what the scanner was built to recognise.
An empty report means that nothing it knows about was found.
questions.onCorrect: A scanner looks for known classes of flaw, so a clean report means only that none of those were found.

choices.label: Yes, if the scanner's database is up to date
Yes, since a scanner checks every part of the code and every library
No, since a scanner finds only flaws of the kinds it knows about

acceptedIdeas: Yes, since a scanner checks every part of the code and every library
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Yes, since a scanner checks every part of the code and every library

misconceptions.feedback: An up-to-date database still holds only flaws already known, and a new flaw in this application's own logic would not be in it.
A scanner looks for the patterns it was built to recognise, and a flaw that matches none of them passes unseen wherever it sits.

questions.prompt: A team ranks flaws with the lesson's rule: the CVSS score times a weight (3 for an internet-facing server, 2 for an internal one, 1 for an isolated one), plus 10 if attacks have been seen. In what order should it patch these five findings, first at the top?
hints: Work out each priority with the rule. The highest priority is patched first.
The score alone does not decide the order. The exposure and the attacks seen are added.

items: Finding X: score 6.5, internet-facing, attacks seen
Finding Y: score 7.8, internal, no attacks seen
Finding Z: score 5.0, internet-facing, no attacks seen
Finding W: score 9.0, isolated, no attacks seen
Finding V: score 8.2, isolated, no attacks seen

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: X scores 6.5 x 3 + 10 = 29.5, Y scores 7.8 x 2 = 15.6, Z scores 5.0 x 3 = 15.0, W scores 9.0 x 1 = 9.0 and V scores 8.2 x 1 = 8.2, so the order is X, Y, Z, W, V.

questions.onCorrect: The 9.0 comes fourth because nobody can reach it, and the 6.5 comes first because it is reachable and already in use.

questions.prompt: A scanner reports a library flaw with a CVSS base score of 9.8 in a tool that runs only on an offline build machine. A colleague says to drop everything. What is the best reply?
hints: CVSS rates the flaw itself. What does it leave out about your own systems?
Compare how many attackers can reach this tool with how many can reach a public server.
questions.onCorrect: The base score rates the technical severity of the flaw. Exposure and evidence of attacks decide the order in which flaws are fixed.

choices.label: Rank it by where the tool runs and whether attacks are seen
Patch it first, because the base score measures the risk to the company
Ignore it, since a flaw on an offline machine cannot matter at all

acceptedIdeas: Rank it by where the tool runs and whether attacks are seen
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Rank it by where the tool runs and whether attacks are seen

misconceptions.feedback: The base score reflects the flaw's intrinsic characteristics. It does not include where the software runs or whether anyone is exploiting it.
A machine that is offline today may be connected tomorrow, and the flaw still gets recorded and fixed. It ranks lower, and it is not ignored.

questions.prompt: A researcher finds a flaw in a company's website and looks for where to send a report. Which published file should tell them?
hints: Think of a file made for vulnerability reports, kept in a well-known place.
RFC 9116 requires a Contact field in it.
questions.onCorrect: RFC 9116 asks web services to place `security.txt` under `/.well-known/`, with a Contact field saying where to send a report.

choices.label: `/robots.txt`, where site owners keep the rules for web crawlers and bots
`/.well-known/security.txt`, where researchers find a contact for reports
`/sitemap.xml`, where site owners list their pages for search engines to read

acceptedIdeas: `/.well-known/security.txt`, where researchers find a contact for reports
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: `/.well-known/security.txt`, where researchers find a contact for reports

misconceptions.feedback: `robots.txt` tells search-engine crawlers which paths to leave alone. It does not say whom to contact about a flaw.
`sitemap.xml` lists pages for search engines and holds no contact for reports.

questions.prompt: Log: 10:01:02 FAIL alice 203.0.113.9, 10:01:05 FAIL alice 203.0.113.9, 10:01:08 FAIL alice 203.0.113.9, 10:01:11 FAIL alice 203.0.113.9, 10:01:14 OK alice 203.0.113.9. What does it most likely show?
hints: Look at the gap between the lines. Would a person mistype at that steady rhythm?
Look at what comes after the failures.
questions.onCorrect: The defender now treats alice's account as compromised and looks at everything it did from 10:01:14 onwards.

choices.label: Alice mistyping her password a few times
Nothing worth following up, since the last attempt succeeded
Automated guessing from one address that succeeded

acceptedIdeas: Automated guessing from one address that succeeded
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Automated guessing from one address that succeeded

misconceptions.feedback: A success after a burst of failures is the point at which an intrusion may begin, so it is the line most worth following up.
The attempts come exactly three seconds apart, a steady machine rhythm that a person correcting a typo would not keep.

questions.prompt: A user logs in from London and, 30 minutes later, from New York, which is 5,570 km away. Roughly how fast would the user have had to travel between the two logins?
hints: Divide the distance by the time, in hours.
Compare the result with the speed of an airliner, about 900 km an hour.
questions.onCorrect: 5,570 km in half an hour is 5,570 ÷ 0.5 = 11,140 km/h, more than ten times an airliner's speed, so the two logins cannot be one person travelling.

choices.label: About as fast as a car on a motorway
About as fast as an airliner
Far faster than any airliner

acceptedIdeas: Far faster than any airliner
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Far faster than any airliner

misconceptions.feedback: At motorway speed, 5,570 km would take more than two days, and the two logins are half an hour apart.
A flight from London to New York takes several hours, and the two logins are only 30 minutes apart.

questions.prompt: A rule fires on 5 or more failures for one account within any 120-second window. Failures for an account occur at 0, 20, 45, 80, 110 and 150 seconds. Does the rule fire?
hints: Slide a 120-second window along the failures and count what falls inside it.
Look for any window that holds five of the six.
questions.onCorrect: The rule fires at 110 seconds, when the fifth failure arrives, without waiting for the sixth.

choices.label: No, since the 120 seconds up to the last failure hold only four
No, since the failures are spread over 150 seconds, longer than the window
Yes, since five of them fall between 0 and 120 seconds

acceptedIdeas: Yes, since five of them fall between 0 and 120 seconds
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Yes, since five of them fall between 0 and 120 seconds

misconceptions.feedback: The rule asks whether any 120 seconds hold five failures, and the stretch from 0 to 120 seconds holds the failures at 0, 20, 45, 80 and 110.
The window is not tied to the last failure. The stretch from 0 to 120 seconds holds five, so the rule fires when the fifth arrives at 110 seconds.

questions.prompt: Why are both times converted to minutes after midnight before they are subtracted?
hints: Compare subtracting 10:25 from 16:50 directly with subtracting two plain numbers.
Which way of writing the two times needs only one subtraction?
questions.onCorrect: 625 and 1010 are plain numbers, so one subtraction gives 385 minutes, and converting back gives 6 hours 25 minutes.

choices.label: Logs record times only as a count of minutes after midnight, in every system
A dwell time has to be measured from midnight to the moment of detection
A single subtraction then gives the gap, with no borrowing across hours

acceptedIdeas: A single subtraction then gives the gap, with no borrowing across hours
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A single subtraction then gives the gap, with no borrowing across hours

misconceptions.feedback: Logs show times such as 10:25. The conversion is a step for the person calculating.
Dwell time runs from the first malicious action to the detection, whenever those fall in the day.

questions.prompt: An intrusion starts at 22:40 and is detected at 03:10 the next morning. What is the dwell time in minutes?
hints: Split the time at midnight.
The part before midnight runs from 22:40 to 24:00.
Add the part before midnight to the part after it.
questions.onCorrect: Splitting at midnight avoids a negative difference when the detection falls on the next day.

misconceptions.feedback: That is only the time after midnight. Add the 80 minutes before it.
That is only the time before midnight. Add the 190 minutes after it.

questions.prompt: An attacker gains administrator access to a web server that keeps the only copy of its log on its own disk. Can the team rely on that log to show what the attacker did?
hints: Ask who can edit a file on that server once they hold administrator rights.
Where would a copy have to be for the attacker to be unable to reach it?
questions.onCorrect: Logs should be sent as written to a separate server that the first machine cannot change, so an intruder cannot edit the record of the visit.

choices.label: No, since an administrator can edit or delete the log to hide a visit
Yes, since every change to a log is itself logged in a second place
Yes, as long as logging was already switched on before the attack began

acceptedIdeas: No, since an administrator can edit or delete the log to hide a visit
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No, since an administrator can edit or delete the log to hide a visit

misconceptions.feedback: Logging being on means the entries were written, but an attacker with administrator rights can change or remove them afterwards.
A log cannot reliably record its own tampering when the person tampering controls the machine that writes it.

questions.prompt: The first malicious activity is at 08:50 and the detection is at 13:35 on the same day. What is the dwell time in minutes?
hints: Convert both times to minutes after midnight, then subtract.
The first malicious activity is at 08:50, which is 530 minutes after midnight.
The detection at 13:35 is 815 minutes after midnight.
questions.onCorrect: Each hour of dwell time is another hour in which the later stages of an intrusion can proceed.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 08:50 is 530 minutes after midnight and 13:35 is 815, so 815 − 530 = 285 minutes, which is 4 hours 45 minutes.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the time in hours. The question asks for minutes.

questions.prompt: One address tries to sign in to 40 different accounts, failing once or twice on each, over two minutes. A rule alerts on 5 failures for one account within two minutes. What would catch this pattern?
hints: Where is the repeated element in this pattern: in one account, or somewhere else?
A threshold counts events within a window. Count the right thing.
questions.onCorrect: A rule counts events grouped by something, and the grouping has to match the pattern. Here it is the source address.

choices.label: The same rule, with the limit lowered from 5 failures to 3
A rule that counts failures from one source address across all accounts
A rule that alerts on every single failed sign-in
A rule that alerts only on successful sign-ins from addresses never seen before

acceptedIdeas: A rule that counts failures from one source address across all accounts
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A rule that counts failures from one source address across all accounts

misconceptions.feedback: No account fails more than twice, so even a limit of 3 never fires. The pattern lies in the address, not in any one account.
That fires on every mistyped password in the company and buries the real signal in noise.
That would catch a success from a new address, but the 40 failures that came first would go unnoticed.

questions.prompt: A rule alerts on every failed sign-in and produces about 4,000 alerts a day. The analysts have started closing them without reading. What is the best fix?
hints: Ask what makes an analyst stop reading alerts.
Which change makes each alert more likely to matter?
questions.onCorrect: Alerts that come to nothing teach analysts to ignore them, so a rule is tuned until the alerts it raises are worth reading.

choices.label: Raise the threshold and add signals, so that fewer and better alerts fire
Hire more analysts until every alert is read, whatever it costs the team
Switch the rule off completely, since nobody acts on the alerts it raises

acceptedIdeas: Raise the threshold and add signals, so that fewer and better alerts fire
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Raise the threshold and add signals, so that fewer and better alerts fire

misconceptions.feedback: More people reading mostly harmless alerts does not make the alerts better. It costs a great deal and the real signal stays buried.
With the rule off, an attack that the rule would catch goes unseen. The fix is to make the rule worth reading.

questions.prompt: Backups run every 6 hours, at 00:00, 06:00, 12:00 and 18:00. Ransomware encrypts the files at 14:20. If the team restores from the latest backup, how many minutes of work are lost?
hints: Find the latest backup before 14:20.
Work out the time from that backup to 14:20.
2 hours is 120 minutes.
questions.onCorrect: The backup schedule sets the most work that a restore can lose, which is why it is settled in preparation.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The latest backup was made at 12:00, and the time from 12:00 to 14:20 is 2 hours 20 minutes, which is 140 minutes.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the time in hours. The question asks for minutes.
That measures from the 06:00 backup. The last backup before the incident was at 12:00.

questions.prompt: Which phase of the lifecycle does isolating the server belong to?
hints: Isolating the server stops the incident growing.
Which phase is about stopping it from growing?
questions.onCorrect: Containment comes before eradication, so that the incident stops growing while the cause is still being found.

acceptedIdeas: containment
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: containment

questions.prompt: A laptop shows a ransom note while the other machines look normal. Which action stops the spread and also keeps what is in the laptop's memory?
hints: Ask what is lost from a machine when it is powered off.
Which choice stops the spread and keeps the evidence?
questions.onCorrect: The machine stays on, so its memory can be captured, and it is cut off, so it can spread nothing.

acceptedIdeas: Isolate it from the network and leave it powered on
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Isolate it from the network and leave it powered on

choices.label: Power it off at once, since an off machine cannot spread anything
Isolate it from the network and leave it powered on
Disable its user's account and leave it connected

misconceptions.feedback: Powering off does stop the spread, but it loses the contents of memory, which may hold the malicious program and its keys. The question asks for both aims.
A disabled account does not disconnect a laptop that is already infected, and the malicious program can still reach other machines.

questions.prompt: During an incident a manager asks the team to wipe a suspected machine at once, to be safe. Is that the right first move?
hints: Ask what a wipe destroys that the team will need later.
If the cause is somewhere else, what would wiping this one machine achieve?
questions.onCorrect: Wiping first loses the evidence of how the attacker got in and the scope of what they touched, and the cause may reinfect the clean machine.

choices.label: Yes, since wiping removes the attacker from the machine and ends the incident
Yes, once a backup of its files has been taken
No, since wiping destroys the evidence, and the cause may remain elsewhere

acceptedIdeas: No, since wiping destroys the evidence, and the cause may remain elsewhere
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No, since wiping destroys the evidence, and the cause may remain elsewhere

misconceptions.feedback: Wiping clears this one machine, but the attacker may hold other machines or a stolen password and can return within the hour.
A copy of the files keeps neither the memory nor the traces of how the attacker got in, and the machine should first be isolated to stop the spread.

questions.prompt: A ransomware alert fires on a file server at 02:00. In what order does a well-run response do these things?
hints: Confirm that something is wrong before acting, and stop the spread before cleaning up.
Evidence is gathered before anything is changed, and the review comes after the service is back.

items: An alert reports files being renamed on the file server
The server is isolated from the network and left powered on
Logs and memory are copied to a separate system
The stolen credential is reset and the malware is removed
The service is restored from a clean backup and watched closely
A blameless review changes how backups are tested

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The alert starts detection, then the server is isolated, the evidence is copied, the cause is eradicated, the service is recovered from a clean backup, and the review follows.

questions.onCorrect: The order follows the lifecycle: detect, contain, preserve, eradicate, recover, and learn, with each step possible only after the one before.

questions.prompt: A team reviews eight actions from one year of incident work. Which phase of the NIST lifecycle does each belong to?
hints: Ask whether each action happens before an incident, while deciding what is happening, while stopping and repairing it, or afterwards.
Restoring from backup belongs to the repair phase, and testing that the backups restore belongs to the preparation.

items.label: Write and rehearse a ransomware runbook
items.explanation: It exists before any incident.

items.label: Test that backups can be restored
items.explanation: The tested backups are ready before they are needed.

items.label: Confirm that an alert is real and list the affected hosts
items.explanation: The team decides what is happening and how far it extends.

items.label: Judge how serious an incident is and open a record
items.explanation: Scoping and recording belong to analysis.

items.label: Disable the account whose password was stolen
items.explanation: It stops the incident growing.

items.label: Restore the server from a clean backup
items.explanation: Recovery returns systems to normal operation.

items.label: Hold a blameless review within days of the end
items.explanation: Lessons learned are drawn after the incident.

items.label: Change a detection rule so the same intrusion is caught earlier
items.explanation: The review feeds the next round of preparation.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The runbook and the backup test are preparation, confirming an alert and judging its seriousness are detection and analysis, disabling the account and restoring the server are containment, eradication and recovery, and the review and the new rule are post-incident activity.

questions.onCorrect: The lifecycle is a loop: what the review learns changes the preparation for the next incident.

questions.prompt: The team has removed the malware from a server, and a manager wants it back online now. The team has not yet found how the attacker got in. What should it do first?
hints: Ask what would happen if the same route were used again the day after restoring.
NIST asks eradication to identify and mitigate the vulnerabilities that were exploited.
questions.onCorrect: Eradication includes closing the route that was used, and recovery then restores service with monitoring turned up.

choices.label: Restore the service now and look for the way in afterwards
Keep the server off until the post-incident review has been held in full
Find and close the way in before restoring, or the attacker may return

acceptedIdeas: Find and close the way in before restoring, or the attacker may return
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Find and close the way in before restoring, or the attacker may return

misconceptions.feedback: A resource that was attacked once is often attacked again, and restoring with the entry route open invites a repeat.
The review happens after recovery. Holding the service until then costs the business time and gains no safety.

questions.prompt: An attacker could change the amount being charged while the request travels to the payment service. Which response deals with that threat?
hints: Changing data on its way is a threat to its integrity.
The worked example dealt with the same threat on flow 1.

acceptedIdeas: An encrypted connection that also detects changes
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: An encrypted connection that also detects changes

questions.onCorrect: The connection detects any change to a message on the way, so a request whose amount was altered fails the check and the payment service rejects it.

choices.label: A limit on how many requests one source may send
A check of the payment service's identity on every connection
An encrypted connection that also detects changes
A record of who placed each order

misconceptions.feedback: A limit on requests answers a flood, which is denial of service. It leaves the contents of a request that is let through untouched.
Checking the service's identity answers spoofing, as in the first line. It does not show whether the amount arrived as it was sent.
A record of who placed each order answers repudiation. It does not stop the amount being changed on the way.

questions.prompt: The last rule in the list denies every packet that the three allow rules above it did not name. Why is the list built that way?
hints: Think about what happens to a service that someone forgot to write a rule for.
Compare the two defaults. Which failure would someone notice and report?
questions.onCorrect: The opposite default, allow unless denied, needs every dangerous flow to be listed in advance, and nobody can list them all.

choices.label: The firewall logs whatever no rule names, so that someone can review it later
A forgotten rule then causes an outage that someone notices, not an exposure
A deny rule outranks every allow rule, so one rule can stop any packet

acceptedIdeas: A forgotten rule then causes an outage that someone notices, not an exposure
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A forgotten rule then causes an outage that someone notices, not an exposure

misconceptions.feedback: Logging records a packet without deciding what happens to it, and a packet that no earlier rule named still needs a decision.
The firewall reads from the top and stops at the first match, so the last rule is reached only by packets that nothing above it matched.

questions.prompt: A program sends the query `SELECT name FROM users WHERE name = ?` and then, separately, the typed value `Ada' OR '1'='1`. How does the database treat that value?
hints: The query text and the value arrive separately.
Think about when the database parsed the query, compared with when the value arrived.

acceptedIdeas: As text to compare with each stored name, quotes included
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: As text to compare with each stored name, quotes included

questions.onCorrect: The quote and the word `OR` are only characters in a text value, so they take no part in how the query is read.

choices.label: As text to compare with each stored name, quotes included
As more of the query, so that the extra condition is applied
As an error, since a name may not contain quotes

misconceptions.feedback: That is what happens when the typed text is joined into the query. Here the query was parsed before the value arrived, so the value cannot add a condition.
A database accepts any characters in a value, quotes included. A quote causes trouble only when the value is joined into the query text.

questions.prompt: Three users sign up, and two of them choose the same password. The site gives each user a fresh random salt before hashing. How many different hash values does it store?
hints: Each user gets a fresh random salt before the password is hashed.
Two inputs that differ in the salt give different digests even when the passwords match.

acceptedIdeas: Three, since each user's salt makes the input different
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Three, since each user's salt makes the input different

questions.onCorrect: Each hash is made from a different input, so cracking one user's password tells the attacker nothing about another user who chose the same one.

choices.label: One, since all three passwords go through the same hash function
Two, since only two different passwords were chosen
Three, since each user's salt makes the input different

misconceptions.feedback: Every password goes through the same function, but the salt makes its input different for each user, so the outputs differ.
That count is right only without salts, where equal passwords give equal hashes. A fresh salt makes the two equal passwords hash to different values.

questions.prompt: Why does the receiver compare the token's audience claim with its own name, `shop-api`?
hints: Ask what could go wrong if a token for one service reached another.
The audience says who the token is for.

acceptedIdeas: A token made for one service should not be accepted by another
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A token made for one service should not be accepted by another

questions.onCorrect: A token that is valid for one service could otherwise be replayed against another, so each receiver accepts only tokens issued for it.

choices.label: The audience names the user who signed in, and the receiver must know who that is
A token made for one service should not be accepted by another
The audience records when the token was issued, which the expiry check needs

misconceptions.feedback: The subject claim names the user. The audience claim is a different claim, and it does not identify a person.
The time of issue is the `iat` claim, and the expiry check uses `exp`. The audience claim records something else.

questions.prompt: A token expires at 1893456000 seconds, and the receiver checks it at 1893457800 seconds. Its signature is valid, and the algorithm, issuer and audience all match. What does the receiver do?
hints: Compare the time of the check with `exp`.
A valid signature says the token is genuine. Does it say the token is current?

acceptedIdeas: It rejects the token, since the time of the check is later than `exp`
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It rejects the token, since the time of the check is later than `exp`

questions.onCorrect: The check fails by half an hour, and one failed check rejects the token however good its signature is.

choices.label: It accepts the token, since the signature is valid and the other claims match
It accepts the token, since it expired only half an hour ago
It rejects the token, since the time of the check is later than `exp`

misconceptions.feedback: A valid signature shows that the token is genuine, not that it is still current.
The check compares two times and has no allowance for a small gap, so half an hour makes no difference to the comparison.

questions.prompt: A token's payload says `"role":"viewer"`. Someone edits the base64url text so that it says `"role":"admin"` and leaves the signature as it was. What happens when the receiver verifies the token?
hints: Think about what the receiver does with the signature before it reads the claims.
Was the signature made over the original payload or the edited one?

acceptedIdeas: The check fails, since the signature was made over the original payload
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The check fails, since the signature was made over the original payload

questions.onCorrect: The receiver recomputes the signature from the payload it received, and an edited payload no longer matches it, which is how a signed token detects changes.

choices.label: The check fails, since the signature was made over the original payload
The token is accepted, since the signature part was left unchanged
The token is accepted, since the receiver checks only the expiry and the claims

misconceptions.feedback: An untouched signature does not make the token valid. The receiver checks it against the payload as it now stands.
The signature check is one of the checks the receiver makes, alongside the checks on the claims.

questions.prompt: Two services share a secret key, and the receiver must be able to detect any message that was made or changed by someone who does not hold it. Which primitive fits?
hints: The services already share a secret key.
Look back at the six primitives listed on the screen about asymmetric cryptography.

acceptedIdeas: A message authentication code
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A message authentication code

questions.onCorrect: The receiver recomputes the fingerprint with the shared key and compares, so a message made or changed by anyone without the key is detected.

choices.label: Key exchange
A plain hash of the whole message
A message authentication code
A slow salted hash

misconceptions.feedback: Key exchange is for agreeing on a shared key, and these services already have one.
A hash has no key, so anyone can compute a fresh fingerprint for a changed message.
A slow salted hash is for storing passwords. It does not use a key shared between sender and receiver.

questions.prompt: A vendor's advisory calls a flaw 'high', but its CVSS base score is 6.8. Which band does 6.8 fall in on the CVSS scale?
hints: Each band covers a range of scores, and the ranges rise from Low to Critical.
The bands change at 4.0, 7.0 and 9.0.
questions.onCorrect: Medium covers 4.0 to 6.9, so a vendor's word 'high' can differ from the band the score falls in.

choices.label: Low
Medium
High
Critical

acceptedIdeas: Medium
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Medium

misconceptions.feedback: Low covers scores from 0.1 to 3.9, and 6.8 is higher than that.
High begins at 7.0, so 6.8 falls just below it.
Critical begins at 9.0.

questions.prompt: A developer wants each log line for a new sign-up to include the user's date of birth and home address, so that support staff can see everything at once. Is that a good idea?
